clinical_manifestations: Discoid plaques with follicular plugging, scarring, and pigment change
Polycyclic photosensitive plaques of subacute disease
Malar erythema of acute disease is a site of lupus, and systemic lupus remains the systemic topic
radiological_manifestations: No routine radiology
pathology_manifestations: Interface dermatitis, basement-membrane thickening, and a lupus band on immunofluorescence
topics.inclusion_rationale: Skin-limited lupus phenotypes with scar and annular photographs. Systemic lupus stays the systemic topic; a malar rash alone is not a topic.

excluded_topics.name: Cardiac Papillary Fibroelastoma
clinical_manifestations: Acute catastrophic neurological embolic presentation: sudden-onset transient ischemic attack (TIA), amaurosis fugax (transient monocular visual loss), acute embolic stroke with hemiparesis or expressive aphasia in young-to-middle-aged patients without conventional atherosclerotic risk factors

Acute coronary embolic presentations: sudden angina, acute myocardial infarction, or sudden cardiac arrest caused by tumor embolization into coronary ostia or dynamic mechanical obstruction of the coronary ostium (especially by aortic valve lesions located directly over the left or right coronary sinuses)

Peripheral cutaneous and vascular embolic signs: splinter hemorrhages beneath the nail beds, painful Osler-like digital ischemic papules, Janeway-like non-tender macular lesions, and acute digital cyanosis / 'blue toe syndrome'
Visceral embolic phenomena: acute sharp flank pain with hematuria from renal infarction, or sudden acute left upper quadrant pain with splenic friction rub from splenic embolization

Auscultatory cardiovascular exam: characteristically benign or unremarkable heart sounds; occasionally a soft, non-radiating systolic murmur or transient clicking sound during leaflet motion, rarely causing hemodynamic valvular dysfunction or regurgitation
radiological_manifestations: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE - Diagnostic Gold Standard): Small (typically <1.5–2.0 cm, mean 10 mm), highly mobile, pedunculated or sessile, round or oval mass with a distinctive speckled, shimmering or 'sea-anemone' border; characteristically attached by a narrow, flexible stalk to the downstream side of valve leaflets (aortic surface of aortic valve [>45%], ventricular surface of mitral valve [>35%], less commonly tricuspid or pulmonary valves); exhibits rapid, independent, chaotic oscillatory motion throughout the cardiac cycle without causing intrinsic valve destruction or significant regurgitation

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): Readily visualizes lesions >5 mm as hyper-echogenic, mobile round masses attached to valve leaflets, distinguishing them from bacterial vegetations by the downstream surface predilection and lack of leaflet destruction

Cardiac MRI (CMR): Small, mobile valvular nodule; isointense to slightly hypointense on T1-weighted images, isointense to hyperintense on T2-weighted sequences; exhibits mild or absent late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) due to paucicellular avascular connective tissue; high temporal resolution SSFP cine imaging demonstrates independent fluttering/motion within the blood pool

High-Resolution Brain MRI (DWI): Multiple, small, punctate, acute cortical and subcortical ischemic lesions scattered across anterior and posterior vascular distributions, reflecting fragmented tumor or fibrin-platelet microemboli
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical Pathology: Pathognomonic appearance when immersed in water/saline: resembles a blooming 'sea anemone' with hundreds of delicate, translucent, gelatinous, shimmering, branching papillary fronds radiating outward from a short, central fibrous stalk; typically measures 0.5–2.0 cm, soft and friable, glistening white to pale yellow, frequently with microscopic surface platelet-fibrin microthrombi

Histopathology: Classic avascular, branching, dendritic papillary fronds lined by a continuous, single layer of normal, flat, CD31-positive endothelial cells; papillary core consists of dense, paucicellular connective tissue enriched with acid mucopolysaccharide ground substance, loose collagen fibers, and prominently curled, wavy, branching elastic fibers (highlighted by Verhoeff-Van Gieson [VVG] elastin stain); complete absence of vascular channels, inflammatory cells, atypia, or mitoses within the frond cores

Distinction from Lambl Excrescences: Giant size (>2 mm vs. minute microscopic ridges), broad distribution on downstream valve surfaces away from the line of closure, and presence of multiple branching arborized fronds
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict criteria by linking dramatic bedside embolic presentations (amaurosis fugax, young stroke, splinter hemorrhages, digital cyanosis) with pathognomonic TEE imaging (small, shimmering, highly mobile mass with fine fronds attached to the downstream valve surface) and gross water-bath 'sea-anemone' pathology with VVG-positive elastin-rich fronds.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Echo and histology only; no clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Chagas Cardiomyopathy
clinical_manifestations: Romaña sign (pathognomonic acute portal sign): unilateral, bipalpebral, painless, violaceous periorbital edema accompanied by non-purulent ipsilateral conjunctivitis and preauricular/submandibular lymphadenopathy (resulting from Trypanosoma cruzi inoculation through the ocular mucous membrane)

Chagoma (inoculation furunculoid lesion): erythematous, indurated, painless or minimally tender inflammatory nodule or plaque at the site of triatomine ('kissing bug') insect vector bite/defecation, often with regional satellite lymphadenopathy
Severe biventricular heart failure signs: massive bilateral lower extremity pitting edema, gross ascites, hepatomegaly with positive hepatojugular reflux, and prominent jugular venous distension
Arrhythmogenic bedside manifestations: severe bradycardia from complete heart block, syncopal episodes (Stokes-Adams attacks), and sudden cardiac death in endemic Latin American regions
Autonomic gastrointestinal phenotypes: severe dysphagia, regurgitation, and cachexia from megaesophagus; intractable constipation and severe abdominal distension with fecaloma from megacolon
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic Echocardiography: Pathognomonic thin-walled, dyskinetic or akinetic left ventricular apical aneurysm (apical nipple / 'kissing' apical lesion) with preserved or hypertrophied basal segments; direct visualization of an apical intra-aneurysmal mural thrombus; severe biventricular dilation, regional wall motion abnormalities affecting the inferolateral wall, and marked reduction in global left ventricular ejection fraction

Cardiac MRI (CMR): Well-defined left ventricular apical thinning and outpouching/aneurysm; transmural or subendocardial late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) localized predominantly to the LV apex and inferolateral basal/mid-ventricular myocardial segments, strongly correlating with life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia substrate

Barium Swallow Esophagogram & Barium Enema CT: Severe dilation, tortuosity, and distal tapering ('bird-beak' sign) of the esophagus (megaesophagus); massive elongation and colonic dilation (megacolon) reflecting systemic myenteric plexus destruction
Chest Radiography: Marked biventricular cardiomegaly ('water-bottle' cardiac silhouette) with pulmonary venous congestion
pathology_manifestations: Gross Cardiac Pathology: Markedly dilated, flabby heart with biventricular chamber enlargement; pathognomonic apical aneurysm characterized by extreme transmural thinning of the LV (and occasionally RV) apex down to 1-2 mm, forming an outpouching lined by fibrous tissue and frequently filled with a laminated mural thrombus

Endomyocardial Biopsy / Autopsy Histopathology: Dense interstitial and perivascular replacement fibrosis with intense mononuclear inflammatory infiltrate (lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells); focal myocyte necrosis and wavy degeneration of myofibers; occasional discovery of intracellular pseudocysts packed with Trypanosoma cruzi amastigotes within cardiac myocytes
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict criteria through classic photographic acute findings (Romaña sign, chagoma), visceral manifestations (megaesophagus/megacolon), and pathognomonic cardiac imaging showing a thinned LV apical aneurysm with apical thrombus on echo/CMR.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Cardiac manifestation of Chagas disease, which is already an infectious-disease topic.

excluded_topics.name: Cor Triatriatum Sinistrum
clinical_manifestations: Mitral stenosis-mimicking presentation: Progressive exertional dyspnea, orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, fatigue, and recurrent episodes of pulmonary edema or hemoptysis secondary to severe pulmonary venous congestion in older children and adults

Auscultatory physical sign: Soft, low-pitched, continuous or mid-to-late diastolic murmur heard at the cardiac apex or lower left sternal border, strikingly differentiated from rheumatic mitral stenosis by the complete absence of an opening snap

Pulmonary hypertension signs: Markedly accentuated, loud pulmonary closure sound (loud P2), palpable pulmonary artery impulse and parasternal lift (right ventricular heave) along the left sternal border

Right heart failure findings: Markedly elevated jugular venous pressure with prominent 'a' waves (reflecting RV noncompliance) or large 'v' waves (from secondary tricuspid regurgitation), tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and dependent peripheral pitting edema in advanced or uncorrected obstruction

Pediatric cyanotic presentation: In infants with a tiny restrictive intra-atrial orifice and coexisting patent foramen ovale (PFO) or atrial septal defect (ASD) communicating with the proximal high-pressure accessory chamber, obligatory right-to-left interatrial shunting produces systemic hypoxemia, central cyanosis, and severe failure to thrive
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic & Transesophageal Echocardiography (TTE/TEE - Modality of Choice): Pathognomonic thin, membranous, or fibromuscular partition (diaphragm) dividing the morphological left atrium into two distinct chambers: a posterosuperior accessory chamber (receiving all four pulmonary veins) and an anteroinferior true left atrium (containing the left atrial appendage, interatrial septum, and mitral valve); Color and continuous-wave Doppler directly demonstrate a high-velocity, turbulent diastolic or continuous jet traversing one or more restrictive fenestrations within the dividing membrane, establishing the trans-membrane gradient and pulmonary hypertension without intrinsic mitral valve structural pathology

Cardiac MRI (CMR): High-resolution steady-state free precession (SSFP) cine sequences unequivocally delineate the insertion lines, thickness, and motility of the intra-atrial fibromuscular membrane, determine the exact location and cross-sectional area of communicating orifices, map pulmonary venous drainage, and quantify right ventricular hypertrophy and pulmonary flow velocities

Cardiac CT Angiography (CTA): High-spatial-resolution 3D volumetric rendering delineates the precise relationship between the pulmonary veins, the accessory left atrial chamber, the anomalous partitioning membrane, the true left atrium, and the coronary sinus, effectively ruling out anomalous pulmonary venous return prior to surgical resection

Chest Radiography: Severe pulmonary venous hypertension with upper lobe blood redistribution ('cephalization' of pulmonary vessels), interstitial Kerley B lines, alveolar pulmonary edema, and prominent main pulmonary artery and right ventricular silhouette, with normal or diminutive left ventricular dimensions and absence of true left atrial body enlargement
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical Pathology: A transverse or oblique fibromuscular, membranous, or diaphragm-like septum subdividing the left atrial cavity into a proximal/superior accessory chamber into which the pulmonary veins empty, and a distal/inferior true chamber that incorporates the left atrial appendage and opens into the mitral orifice; the membrane contains one or multiple central or eccentric perforations (fenestrations) that range from pinhole orifices (< 3 mm) producing lethal infantile obstruction to wide openings (> 10 mm) presenting late in life

Histopathology: The intra-atrial partition is composed of a dense fibrous or fibromuscular core containing haphazardly oriented smooth muscle cells and elastic laminae, covered on both the proximal and distal surfaces by a continuous layer of vascular endothelial cells; high-pressure proximal accessory atrial myocardium exhibits prominent compensatory muscular hypertrophy and dense endocardial fibroelastosis, whereas the distal true left atrial wall remains thin and unremodeled
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic structural membrane anomaly mimicking rheumatic mitral stenosis without an opening snap, diagnosed by the pathognomonic intra-atrial fibromuscular membrane partitioning the left atrium on echocardiography/CMR with turbulent trans-membrane Doppler acceleration, and confirmed by characteristic diaphragmatic histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Imaging diagnosis (echo/CT) without a disease-specific external image.

excluded_topics.name: Intrapericardial Teratoma
clinical_manifestations: Fetal and neonatal hydrops photographic appearance: massive generalized anasarca (scalp edema, severe subcutaneous fluid accumulation across torso and limbs), profound ascites, pleural effusions, and marked abdominal protuberance in the newborn

Neonatal acute cardiac tamponade signs: profound hypotension, weak/thready peripheral pulses, mottled cool extremities, marked cyanosis, and severe respiratory distress (grunting, tachypnea, severe intercostal retractions)

Bedside physical signs of great vessel compression: prominent non-pulsatile distension of jugular and scalp veins from superior vena cava obstruction; stridor and tracheal tugging from extrinsic airway compression

Auscultatory physical examination: muffled, distant, or barely audible heart tones (due to massive pericardial fluid insulation), lack of audible murmurs or faint systolic murmurs over the base, and severe tachycardia (>180–200 bpm)

Abdominal bedside physical exam: striking, tender hepatomegaly extending multiple centimeters below the right costal margin with marked hepatojugular reflux, reflecting acute right atrial collapse and venous congestion
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic & Fetal Echocardiography (Primary Bedside Imaging Hallmark): Complex, multilocular, heterogeneous intrapericardial mass typically attached by a broad or narrow pedicle to the root of the ascending aorta or pulmonary trunk at the pericardial reflection; mass contains distinct hypoechoic cystic cavities interspersed with hyperechoic solid components and bright echogenic acoustic shadows (calcifications); associated massive circumferential pericardial effusion with severe hemodynamic tamponade (diastolic compression and collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle, superior vena cava obstruction)

Chest CT (High-Resolution Non-Contrast & Contrast-Enhanced): Pathognomonic multilocular, lobulated intrapericardial lesion demonstrating classic 'three-germ-layer' tissue attenuation: fluid/cystic attenuation (0–20 HU), macroscopic fat density (-50 to -100 HU), soft tissue elements (30–50 HU), and coarse, punctate or curvilinear dense calcifications (>100 HU); precise depiction of extrinsic compression on the aorta, pulmonary artery, superior vena cava, and trachea

Fetal and Neonatal Cardiac MRI (CMR): Large, well-encapsulated intrapericardial mass with heterogeneous signal intensity across sequences; hyperintense signal on T1-weighted images suppressing on fat-saturated sequences confirms macroscopic lipid/fat content; hyperintense fluid signals on T2-weighted images corresponding to cystic spaces; heterogeneous late gadolinium enhancement in solid components

Chest Radiography (CXR): Massive, globular enlargement of the cardiothoracic silhouette ('water-bottle' heart) in the neonate, filling the entire hemithorax, with displacement of the trachea and bronchus and attenuation of lung markings
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical Pathology: Large (often 4–10 cm in diameter, often dwarfing the neonatal heart), multi-lobulated, encapsulated mass enveloped by smooth, glistening fibrous capsule; cut surface reveals a variegated appearance composed of multiple fluid-filled cysts containing clear, serous, mucinous, or sebaceous fluid, interspersed with solid yellowish-white cartilage-like tissue, gritty calcific nodules, and adipose tissue; pedicle consistently arises from the adventitia of the ascending aorta near the transverse pericardial sinus

Histopathology (Tridermic Elements): Mature, benign tissues derived from all three embryonic germ layers: Ectoderm (stratified squamous epithelium with keratin, hair follicles, sebaceous glands, neural/glial tissue), Mesoderm (mature hyaline cartilage, adipose tissue, bone, smooth muscle bundles, loose mesenchymal connective tissue), and Endoderm (respiratory pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells, gastrointestinal enteric epithelium, pancreatic acini); absence of immature neuroepithelial rosettes in benign mature teratomas
Pericardial Fluid Analysis: Massive non-hemorrhagic serous, serosanguinous, or xanthochromic transudate/exudate with markedly elevated total protein and high alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) concentrations
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Satisfies strict multimodal visual criteria by uniting striking bedside neonatal features (hydrops fetalis anasarca, scalp edema, severe tamponade, SVC distension) with pathognomonic imaging (fetal/neonatal echo showing a heterogeneous multilocular mass attached to the aortic root with massive effusion, and CT showing fat, calcium, and cystic attenuation), verified by tridermic mature teratoma histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Fetal/surgical imaging mass without a bedside clinical image.

excluded_topics.name: Left Ventricular Non-Compaction Cardiomyopathy
clinical_manifestations: Clinical triad of LVNC: progressive heart failure, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, and systemic thromboembolic events (stroke, transient ischemic attack, mesenteric ischemia, peripheral arterial occlusion)

Bedside signs of advanced biventricular congestive heart failure: cold, pale, mottled peripheries; anasarca; elevated jugular venous pressure with giant v waves; hepatomegaly; laterally displaced, diffuse, hyperdynamic apical impulse with palpable pre-systolic impulse (S4) or protodiastolic gallop (S3)

Neuromuscular and syndromic dysmorphisms (in familial and mitochondrial forms, e.g. Barth syndrome): facial dysmorphisms (round face, prominent cheeks), growth retardation, digital clubbing in pediatric presentation, skeletal muscle weakness, and exercise intolerance
Peripheral embolic signs: acute cold, pale, pulseless extremity (acute limb ischemia) or focal neurological deficits from cardiogenic cerebral emboli originating in deep intertrabecular recesses
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic & Contrast Echocardiography: Pathognomonic two-layered myocardial architecture consisting of a thin compacted epicardial layer and an excessively thickened, deeply trabeculated non-compacted endocardial layer (primarily involving the LV apex, lateral wall, and inferior wall); Jenni diagnostic criteria: end-systolic ratio of non-compacted to compacted myocardium (NC/C) > 2.0; Color Doppler demonstrating deep intertrabecular recesses communicating directly with the left ventricular cavity (perfused by intracavitary blood flow without communication with the coronary circulation); direct visualization of thrombi lodged within the deep recesses

Cardiac MRI (CMR - Diagnostic Gold Standard): Petersen criteria: end-diastolic ratio of non-compacted to compacted myocardium (NC/C) > 2.3 measured in long-axis views; Jacquier criteria: non-compacted myocardial mass index > 20% of total LV myocardial mass; high-resolution cine SSFP sequences displaying prominent spongy hypertrabeculation with deep crypts; late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) often present in trabeculae and subendocardial compacted myocardium indicating replacement fibrosis
Left Ventriculography: 'Spongy' appearance of the apical and inferolateral myocardium with persistence of radiographic contrast medium in deep crypts during diastole and systole
pathology_manifestations: Gross Cardiac Pathology: Markedly spongy, honeycomb-like endocardial surface with numerous prominent muscular trabeculae (>3) and deep intertrabecular fissures extending deep toward the thin outer compacted epicardial layer; prominent absence or disorganization of the normal apical papillary muscle architecture; frequent organized mural thrombi sequestered in the recesses

Histopathology: Non-compacted layer demonstrates hypertrophied and degenerating myocytes with irregular orientation; prominent endocardial fibroelastosis lining the intertrabecular recesses; interstitial fibrosis; electron microscopy showing mitochondrial abnormalities and disrupted sarcomeric Z-discs
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict criteria: clear bedside thromboembolic and heart failure phenotypes linked with the pathognomonic visual two-layered 'spongiform' myocardium (NC/C ratio >2.3 on CMR, deep recesses filled by color Doppler on echo) and characteristic gross honeycomb pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Echocardiographic/MRI diagnosis without pathognomonic clinical photographs.

excluded_topics.name: Libman-Sacks Endocarditis (SLE & Antiphospholipid Syndrome)
clinical_manifestations: Cutaneous hallmarks of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): malar (butterfly) erythema over the nasal bridge and cheeks sparing the nasolabial folds, photosensitive discoid erythematous plaques with follicular plugging, and periungual telangiectasias

Cutaneous and vascular stigmata of secondary antiphospholipid syndrome (APS): extensive livedo reticularis (violaceous, reticulated, lace-like mottled vascular pattern of the lower extremities and torso), splinter hemorrhages under nail beds, and painful digital cutaneous necrosis/ulcerations

Auscultatory physical findings: newly emergent holosystolic regurgitant murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla (mitral regurgitation) or high-pitched early diastolic decrescendo murmur along the left sternal border (aortic regurgitation), frequently fluctuating in intensity over time

Peripheral thromboembolic physical signs: acute cerebral ischemia presenting as focal neurological deficits (transient ischemic attack, acute stroke), amaurosis fugax, or painful violaceous peripheral emboli to digits ('blue toe syndrome')

Constitutional and musculoskeletal features: low-grade remittent fever, symmetrical non-deforming polyarthritis/arthralgias involving small joints of the hands and wrists, non-scarring alopecia, and painless oral/nasopharyngeal aphthous ulcerations
radiological_manifestations: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE - Gold Standard Modality): Pathognomonic small-to-moderate (usually 2–10 mm), broad-based, sessile, verrucous or irregularly shaped nodular non-bacterial vegetations adhering characteristically to BOTH the atrial and ventricular surfaces of the mitral valve leaflets (especially the posterior leaflet) and the aortic valve cusps; lack of independent oscillatory motion or leaflet destruction (distinguishing from bacterial endocarditis); associated diffuse valve leaflet thickening and variable degrees of regurgitation

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): Demonstration of valvular thickening, irregular leaflet margins, regurgitant color Doppler jets across mitral and aortic orifices, and assessment of concomitant pericardial effusion or lupus myocarditis with global longitudinal strain reduction

Cardiac MRI (CMR): Thickened, irregular mitral/aortic leaflets with patchy, delayed late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) reflecting active valve inflammation and fibrovascular repair; cine SSFP imaging demonstrates turbulent regurgitant jets and quantifies regurgitant fraction; concurrent evaluation of transmural or mid-wall myocardial inflammation and pericardial late enhancement in active lupus carditis

Brain MRI (Diffusion-Weighted Imaging [DWI]): Multiple, punctate or wedge-shaped acute cerebral infarctions in non-contiguous arterial territories ('shower of emboli' pattern) secondary to detached non-bacterial thrombotic-verrucous debris
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical / Autopsy Pathology: Small (1–10 mm), firm, dry, sterile, grayish-yellow to reddish-brown verrucous vegetations, either solitary or clustered, distributed atypically on both sides of the valve leaflets (atrial and ventricular aspects), extending along the lines of closure, onto the subvalvular apparatus, commissures, chordae tendineae, and adjacent mural endocardium

Histopathology: Triphasic structural progression—active phase shows superficial accumulations of eosinophilic fibrin, platelets, and entrapped immunoglobulins, surrounded by subendothelial cellular infiltration with lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes; pathognomonic basophilic hematoxylin bodies (altered nuclear chromatin from LE cells); intermediate healing phase reveals abundant neo-vascularization, active fibroblastic proliferation, and inflammatory granulation; healed phase demonstrates dense, acellular collagenous fibrous scarring with leaflet distortion

Immunofluorescence: Granular subendothelial and vascular basement membrane deposits of immunoglobulins (IgG, IgM, IgA) and complement components (C3, C1q, C4d) along the valve surface and microvessels, confirming immune-complex pathogenesis
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Satisfies strict multimodal visual criteria by uniting striking bedside cutaneous stigmata (SLE malar rash, discoid lupus, livedo reticularis, splinter hemorrhages) with pathognomonic transesophageal echocardiography showing bilateral, sessile verrucous vegetations on both leaflet surfaces without leaflet destruction, and hallmark histopathology demonstrating hematoxylin bodies and immune-complex deposition.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Manifestation of SLE / antiphospholipid syndrome, both already topics. Valvular vegetations are a finding, not a separate image-library disease.

excluded_topics.name: Non-Bacterial Thrombotic Endocarditis (NBTE / Marantic Endocarditis)
clinical_manifestations: Paraneoplastic and wasting stigmata: severe cancer cachexia, temporal muscle wasting, sunken eyes, dry pale skin, and profound asthenia in patients with underlying advanced mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas (pancreas, lung, colon, ovary)

Acute catastrophic arterial embolic bedside presentation: sudden-onset dense focal neurological deficits (hemiplegia, aphasia, homonymous hemianopsia from massive embolic stroke) in over 50% of cases, often the initial clinical harbinger of covert visceral malignancy

Peripheral visceral and extremity embolic physical signs: sudden acute severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs from acute mesenteric ischemia / splenic infarction, sudden flank pain with gross hematuria from renal infarction, or sudden acute cold, pulseless, pale, painful limb (acute extremity ischemia / saddle embolus)

Cutaneous embolic markers: splinter hemorrhages in nail beds, subungual petechiae, digital gangrene/cyanosis, and migratory superficial thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) with palpable, tender, erythematous cord-like veins across the extremities

Auscultatory cardiovascular exam: quiet heart examination, frequently with soft, newly variable systolic flow or regurgitant murmurs (mitral > aortic) that may fluctuate or be completely absent despite large mobile vegetations
radiological_manifestations: Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE - Diagnostic Imaging Modality of Choice): Highly mobile, irregularly shaped, wide-based or pedunculated, friable vegetations located along the coaptation lines of closure on the atrial surface of the mitral valve (most common) or ventricular surface of the aortic valve; striking absence of valve tissue destruction, perforation, abscess, or aneurysm (distinguishing it from active bacterial infective endocarditis); vegetations often easily fragment during cardiac cycles

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): Lower sensitivity (40–50%) for small friable lesions, but visualizes larger mobile masses, assesses valve leaflet coaptation, regurgitation jets with color Doppler, and rules out ventricular dysfunction

Diffusion-Weighted Brain MRI (DWI / ADC): Widespread, bilateral, multiple territorial and watershed cortical and subcortical acute diffusion-restricted infarcts of varying sizes ('embolic rain' or 'multi-territory thromboembolism'), pathognomonic for central cardioembolic seeding from uncalcified cardiac vegetations

Contrast-Enhanced Chest/Abdominal CT: Detection of occult mucin-secreting primary visceral neoplasm (e.g., pancreatic adenocarcinoma, bronchogenic carcinoma) combined with sharp wedge-shaped non-enhancing hypodensities in the spleen, kidneys, or mesenteric arterial occlusion; concomitant deep venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism
pathology_manifestations: Gross Autopsy / Surgical Pathology: Friable, yellowish-tan to reddish-brown, cauliflower-like or nodular vegetations ranging from microscopic to >15 mm along the coaptation margins of valve leaflets; strikingly loose endocardial attachment allowing effortless detachment (high embolic propensity) without underlying leaflet erosion, excavation, or perforation

Histopathology: Sterile accumulations of aggregated platelets and laminated bands of eosinophilic fibrin interwoven with sparse erythrocytes; conspicuous and complete absence of inflammatory cellular infiltration (virtually no neutrophils, lymphocytes, or histiocytes at the base) and complete absence of microorganisms on Gram, Gomori methenamine silver (GMS), and Periodic acid–Schiff (PAS) stains; minimal or absent organizing fibroblastic response at the attachment zone
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict criteria by linking profound bedside clinical findings (severe cachexia, Trousseau migratory thrombophlebitis, sudden multi-territory embolic stroke, peripheral ischemic gangrene) with distinctive TEE findings of friable, mobile vegetations along lines of closure without valvular destruction, confirmed by sterile, non-inflammatory platelet-fibrin thrombus pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Manifestation of malignancy or antiphospholipid syndrome, not an independent photographic disease.

excluded_topics.name: Patent Ductus Arteriosus with Eisenmenger Syndrome
excluded_topics.subspecialty: Congenital Heart Disease & Pulmonary Vascular Diseases
clinical_manifestations: Pathognomonic differential cyanosis: vivid visual contrast where the toes and lower extremities display marked cyanosis (dusky, bluish-purple discoloration), whereas the fingers and upper extremities (most strikingly the right hand) remain normally oxygenated, pink, and healthy; occurs because unoxygenated blood shunts right-to-left from the pulmonary artery through the ductus arteriosus directly into the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery

Pathognomonic differential digital clubbing: pronounced bulbous clubbing of the toenails accompanied by normal, unclubbed fingernails (or isolated left fingernail clubbing if the ductus enters near the left subclavian artery, with completely spared right hand)

Bedside signs of severe pulmonary arterial hypertension: loud, palpable, single or narrowly split pulmonary component of the second heart sound (P2); palpable pulmonary artery heave in the second left intercostal space; high-pitched early diastolic Graham Steell decrescendo murmur of pulmonary regurgitation
Secondary erythrocytosis signs: plethoric facies, suffused conjunctival vessels, hyperuricemic tophi, and hemoptysis from ruptured dilated bronchial collateral vessels
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography: Massive, aneurysmal dilatation of the main pulmonary artery trunk and hilar pulmonary branches ('pulmonary knob' bulging prominent left cardiac waist), paired with abrupt tapering and disappearance of peripheral pulmonary vasculature ('pruning' or 'peripheral oligemia'); prominent right ventricular enlargement

Transthoracic & Bubble-Contrast Echocardiography: Direct visualization of a large, widely patent ductus arteriosus between the aortic isthmus and the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery; color Doppler demonstrates right-to-left or bidirectional shunt across the ductus; agitated saline contrast (bubble study) injected into an upper extremity vein shows immediate appearance of microbubbles in the descending abdominal aorta while completely sparing the ascending aorta and carotid vessels; severe concentric right ventricular hypertrophy with flattened/paradoxical ventricular septal motion ('D-shaped' left ventricle)

CT Angiography (CTA) / MR Angiography (MRA) of the Chest: Exquisite 3D demonstration of the persistent patent ductus arteriosus with dense mural calcification of the ductus and pulmonary trunk; massive aneurysmal main pulmonary artery (often >40-50 mm); severe peripheral pulmonary arteriolar pruning
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology: Wide, tubular, or window-type persistent ductus arteriosus connecting the pulmonary artery trunk to the descending aorta with thickened, calcified, atherosclerotic walls; extreme concentric right ventricular hypertrophy with RV wall thickness equaling or exceeding the left ventricular myocardium; marked dilation of the pulmonary trunk

Histopathology (Heath-Edwards Grade IV-VI plexogenic pulmonary arteriopathy): Concentric laminar intimal fibrosis of small pulmonary muscular arteries and arterioles ('onion-skin' intimal proliferation); pathognomonic plexiform lesions (aneurysmal dilatation of thin-walled vessels lined by proliferating endothelial channels); necrotizing arteritis with fibrinoid necrosis and transmural inflammatory infiltrate in terminal stages
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict criteria: boasts one of medicine's most legendary bedside photographic findings — differential cyanosis and differential clubbing (cyanotic clubbed toes vs. pink normal right hand) — paired with aneurysmal pulmonary pruning on chest X-ray/CTA and right-to-left ductal shunting on echo.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Eisenmenger physiology is a complication of shunt lesions, not a standalone topic.

excluded_topics.name: Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava
synonyms: Duplication of the superior vena cava
Left superior vena cava draining into coronary sinus
clinical_manifestations: Catheterization/procedure misdirection: Striking procedural discovery during left subclavian or internal jugular vein central venous catheterization, pulmonary artery catheterization, or cardiac implantable electronic device (pacemaker/ICD) lead placement: the catheter or lead follows an unexpected left paramediastinal downward vertical course instead of crossing the midline via the innominate vein

Cyanotic presentation in unroofed variants: In ~10% of cases where the PLSVC drains anomalously directly into the left atrium (associated with an unroofed coronary sinus or absent coronary sinus roof), patients present with central cyanosis, digital clubbing, exertional dyspnea, and recurrent paradoxical systemic arterial thromboembolism (cryptogenic ischemic stroke, cerebral abscess)

Cardiac rhythm disturbances: Palpitations, sinus node dysfunction, sick sinus syndrome, supraventricular tachyarrhythmias (atrial flutter/fibrillation), and varying degrees of atrioventricular block caused by chronic stretching and compression of the atrioventricular junction and nodal tissue by the massively dilated coronary sinus

Physical examination in isolated cases: Typically normal on routine bedside exam when drainage is into the right atrium; in unroofed left atrial drainage, bedside exam demonstrates resting mucosal cyanosis without pulmonary distress, prominent digital clubbing, and a soft systolic murmur
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE - Initial Diagnostic Indicator): Pathognomonic finding of a markedly dilated coronary sinus (CS) visualized in the parasternal long-axis view as a prominent, circular, echo-free lumen in the posterior atrioventricular groove (normal CS diameter < 10 mm; in PLSVC typically > 15-25 mm); apical 4-chamber and modified views confirm massive CS enlargement

Confirmatory Agitated Saline Bubble Study (Acoustic Contrast Test): Injected agitated saline into a LEFT antecubital vein produces rapid, immediate opacification of the dilated coronary sinus FIRST, followed by opacification of the right atrium; conversely, agitated saline injected into a RIGHT antecubital vein produces normal physiological opacification of the right atrium directly before the coronary sinus, definitively confirming PLSVC draining into the coronary sinus (in unroofed coronary sinus variants, left-arm bubble injection results in immediate opacification of the left atrium and left ventricle)

Contrast-Enhanced Chest CT / CTA: Unmistakable 3D demonstration of a persistent vertical venous channel descending on the left lateral border of the mediastinum, passing anterior to the left pulmonary hilum and lateral to the aortic arch, draining into the coronary sinus along the posterior AV groove; clearly evaluates presence or absence of a bridging left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein and status of the right SVC (bilateral SVCs present in ~80-90%)

Cardiac MRI (CMR): Multiplanar SSFP cine and 3D phase-contrast MR venography clearly visualize the full systemic venous course, definitively assess the integrity of the coronary sinus roof, and quantify right-to-left or left-to-right shunt fractions in complex congenital associations

Fluoroscopy & Chest Radiography: Catheter, guidewire, or pacing lead advanced from the left subclavian vein forms a characteristic left-sided vertical paramediastinal stripe along the left upper mediastinal border before looping through the coronary sinus into the right atrium or ventricle
pathology_manifestations: Gross Anatomy & Pathology: Embryological failure of normal involution of the proximal portion of the left anterior cardinal vein and the left horn of the sinus venosus (which normally involutes into the ligament of Marshall); a large venous vessel descends vertically anterior to the left aortic arch, traverses the left pericardial reflection, passes anterior to the left pulmonary veins, and courses along the posterior left atrioventricular groove as a gigantic, tortuous, thin-walled coronary sinus before entering the right atrium between the IVC and tricuspid valve; in unroofed coronary sinus syndrome, there is a fenestration or complete absence of the partition between the coronary sinus and the left atrium

Histopathology: Normal three-layered venous histological architecture (endothelial intima, thin muscular media with circular smooth muscle fibers, and fibrous adventitia) of the left superior vena cava, with secondary eccentric fibromuscular hypertrophy, elastic tissue fragmentation, and fibrous remodeling in the wall of the chronically volume-loaded coronary sinus
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Commonest congenital thoracic systemic venous malformation featuring signature central catheter misdirection and cyanosis in unroofed variants, verified by the pathognomonic dilated coronary sinus on TTE with diagnostic retrograde left-arm agitated saline bubble progression, and classic embryological cardinal vein persistence.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Anatomic venous variant. Diagnosis is catheter or CT position, with no clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Pulmonary Artery Intimal Sarcoma
synonyms: Malignant intimal sarcoma of the pulmonary artery
clinical_manifestations: Subacute progressive right ventricular failure signs: profound jugular venous distension with giant 'a' waves (reflecting high RV end-diastolic pressure) and steep 'v' waves, tender pulsatile hepatomegaly, massive lower extremity pitting edema, and ascites in patients mistakenly treated for weeks or months for 'recurrent unresolving pulmonary embolism'

Auscultatory physical findings: loud, palpable, single or narrowly split second heart sound (P2) heard over the left upper sternal border; harsh systolic ejection murmur in the second left intercostal space that increases with inspiration (Carvallo-like behavior) caused by flow acceleration across the obstructed pulmonary trunk; right-sided S3 and S4 gallops

Bedside respiratory manifestations: worsening exertional dyspnea, episodic hemoptysis (from pulmonary infarction or bronchial artery collateral hypertrophy), orthopnea, pleuritic chest pain, and frequent syncopal episodes provoked by minimal exertion

Paraneoplastic and systemic constitutional features: significant involuntary weight loss, cancer cachexia, clubbing of the fingers and toes (hypertrophic osteoarthropathy), intermittent pyrexia, and absence of deep vein thrombosis (negative lower extremity venous Duplex ultrasound)
Diagnostic physical trap: lack of clinical improvement, progression of symptoms, and worsening hemodynamic collapse despite full therapeutic anticoagulation
radiological_manifestations: Contrast-Enhanced Computed Tomography Angiography (CTA - Hallmark Imaging Modality): Expansile, lobulated, polypoid filling defect completely filling and expanding the lumen of the main pulmonary artery trunk, extending across the bifurcation into right and left main pulmonary arteries; pathognomonic signs distinguishing it from thromboembolism: marked luminal expansion of the pulmonary artery (PA diameter greater than adjacent aorta), extravascular or transmural invasion through the vessel wall into mediastinum, right ventricular outflow tract, or lung parenchyma, and conspicuous, heterogeneous contrast enhancement within the mass during the arterial phase

Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance (CMR): Hyperintense, expansile intraluminal mass on T2-weighted and STIR images; intense, early and late heterogeneous contrast enhancement on late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) imaging confirming high vascularity and viable malignant tissue (whereas thromboemboli are avascular and show zero contrast enhancement); evaluates right ventricular dilatation, hypertrophy, and ejection fraction

18F-FDG PET-CT (Definitive Metabolic Discriminator): Intense, avid, hypermetabolic FDG uptake (SUVmax typically >6.0 to 20.0) localized to the pulmonary artery mass, conclusively distinguishing viable malignant intimal sarcoma from photopenic, metabolically inert chronic thromboemboli; identifies distant metastases

Transthoracic & Transesophageal Echocardiography (TTE/TEE): Direct visualization of a mobile or sessile mass obstructing the RVOT and pulmonary valve orifice, protruding into the main pulmonary trunk; severe pulmonary hypertension with right ventricular systolic pressure (RVSP) >60–80 mmHg, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and McConnell sign or RV dilatation
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical / Autopsy Pathology: Soft, fleshy, gelatinous, polypoid, gray-white to yellowish-tan intravascular mass arising directly from the intimal lining of the pulmonary trunk; firmly attached to the vessel wall, expanding the arterial lumen, with focal areas of hemorrhage, necrosis, and mucoid degeneration, often propagating distally into lobar and segmental pulmonary branches

Histopathology: Undifferentiated, highly pleomorphic, atypical spindle and polygonal malignant mesenchymal cells arranged in fascicles, storiform patterns, or sheets; marked nuclear atypia, hyperchromasia, multinucleated tumor giant cells, frequent atypical mitoses, and myxoid or collagenous extracellular matrix; lacks specific intrinsic vascular, muscular, or neural differentiation, although focal osteosarcomatous, chondrosarcomatous, or rhabdomyoblastic heterologous elements may occur

Immunohistochemistry & Molecular Genetics: Characteristically shows diffuse, strong nuclear immunoreactivity for MDM2 and CDK4; high-level genomic amplification of the 12q12-15 chromosomal region (containing MDM2 and CDK4 genes by FISH or NGS, pathognomonic molecular hallmark); positive for osteopontin and vimentin; negative for endothelial markers CD31, ERG, and kerato-epithelial markers
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Meets strict multimodal visual criteria by pairing bedside signs (refractory RV failure, loud P2 murmur, digital clubbing, lack of response to anticoagulation) with pathognomonic CTA/CMR findings (luminal expansion of the pulmonary trunk, extravascular invasion, heterogeneous contrast enhancement) and intense FDG PET avidity, confirmed by MDM2/CDK4-amplified intimal sarcoma pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: CT/PET vascular filling defect without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Sinus of Valsalva Aneurysm
clinical_manifestations: Acute rupture presentation: Sudden, catastrophic onset of severe retrosternal or epigastric tearing chest pain, acute dyspnea, and rapid collapse into acute right heart failure or cardiogenic shock, often triggered by physical exertion or coughing

Auscultatory pathognomonic sign: Loud, harsh, continuous 'machinery-like' or 'sawing' murmur heard along the left and right sternal borders, characteristically louder in diastole than in systole, accompanied by a palpable continuous precordial thrill

Peripheral hyperdynamic arterial signs: Marked widening of pulse pressure with classic bounding 'water-hammer' (Corrigan) peripheral pulses, visible capillary pulsations in nail beds (Quincke sign), pistol-shot sounds over femoral arteries (Traube sign), and systolic/diastolic femoral murmurs with compression (Duroziez sign), mimicking severe acute aortic regurgitation

Acute right heart failure signs upon intracardiac rupture: Massive, sudden elevation of jugular venous pressure with towering 'v' waves and prominent pulsations, acute painful tender hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral pitting edema due to high-volume left-to-right aorto-cardiac shunting into the right ventricle or right atrium

Unruptured presentation: Asymptomatic incidental finding or slowly progressive dyspnea, conduction system arrhythmias (complete heart block from mechanical compression of the bundle of His/AV node by a non-coronary sinus aneurysm), myocardial ischemia from extrinsic coronary artery compression, or right ventricular outflow tract obstruction
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic & Transesophageal Echocardiography (TTE/TEE - Gold Standard Diagnostic Modality): Direct visualization of a thin-walled, saccular, or tubular aneurysmal outpouching originating from an aortic sinus (most commonly right coronary sinus [65-85%], followed by non-coronary sinus [10-30%], rarely left coronary sinus [<5%]); pathognomonic mobile 'windsock' deformity protruding into the right ventricle (from right coronary sinus) or right atrium (from non-coronary sinus); Color Doppler definitively confirms rupture by demonstrating a continuous, turbulent, high-velocity jet flowing directly from the aorta into the receiving low-pressure cardiac chamber, with secondary aortic valve regurgitation or prolapse

Multidetector CT Angiography (MDCTA): Exceptional 3D volumetric depiction of the aortic root, precisely detailing the exact sinus of origin, neck dimensions, length and trajectory of the 'windsock' sac, specific rupture site/perforation, relationship to coronary artery ostia, and identification of coexisting congenital anomalies (ventricular septal defect present in 30-50% of cases)

Cardiac MRI (CMR): Cine SSFP sequences visualize dynamic, pulsatile systolic-diastolic expansion of the windsock sac; phase-contrast velocity-encoded imaging quantifies the magnitude of the continuous left-to-right shunt (Qp:Qs pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio); late gadolinium enhancement assesses right ventricular remodeling and strain

Aortography (Invasive Cardiac Catheterization): Contrast injection into the aortic root demonstrates immediate, dramatic opacification of the aneurysmal sac followed instantaneously by dense opacification of the receiving right heart chamber (right ventricle or right atrium) through the fistulous tract

Chest Radiography: Progressive biventricular cardiomegaly, marked enlargement of the ascending aortic contour, and dramatic pulmonary plethora / vascular engorgement caused by massive acute left-to-right intracardiac shunting
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical Pathology: A thin-walled, pouch-like or tubular saccular protrusion of the aortic sinus extending into an adjacent cardiac chamber; in ruptured cases, the blind end of the pouch shows a ragged perforation, slit-like tear, or multiple cribriform fenestrations ('pepper-pot' appearance) forming an aortocardiac fistula directly communicating with the right ventricle, right atrium, or rarely pulmonary artery or pericardium

Histopathology: Localized congenital absence, defect, or marked attenuation of the normal elastic tissue and smooth muscle architecture of the aortic tunica media at the junction where the aortic wall joins the fibrous annulus of the aortic valve; the aneurysmal wall consists almost entirely of attenuated, hyalinized collagenous fibrous tissue and layered endocardium lacking internal elastic laminae, showing secondary myxoid degeneration, elastic fiber fragmentation, and mural thrombi
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Dramatic acute structural aorto-cardiac catastrophe with classic physical exam signs (continuous machinery murmur, bounding water-hammer pulses, acute right heart failure), pathognomonic 'windsock' outpouching with high-velocity continuous color jet on TEE/CTA, and diagnostic histological congenital deficiency of aortic media at the valve annulus.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Echo/CT/angiographic lesion without a disease-specific photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Takotsubo Cardiomyopathy
clinical_manifestations: Precipitating stress trigger: Acute, profound physical stressor (e.g., acute intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic stroke, sepsis, status epilepticus, severe trauma, major non-cardiac surgery, severe asthma) or catastrophic emotional stressor (e.g., sudden bereavement, severe divorce, catastrophic financial loss, acute robbery/fright) immediately preceding symptom onset, overwhelmingly occurring in postmenopausal women (>90%)

Acute coronary syndrome presentation: Sudden onset of severe, crushing substernal chest pain, acute dyspnea, profuse diaphoresis, palpitations, and presyncope/syncope clinically indistinguishable from acute anterior ST-elevation myocardial infarction

Hemodynamic and heart failure signs: Hypotension, acute pulmonary edema with bilateral basilar rales, S3 gallop, and cardiogenic shock (occurring in ~10% of cases, mediated by acute left ventricular systolic failure or dynamic left ventricular outflow tract obstruction)

Auscultatory dynamic murmur: Transient, harsh, mid-systolic ejection murmur heard at the lower left sternal border and cardiac apex in patients who develop dynamic LVOT obstruction due to compensatory basal hyperkinesis and systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve

Electrocardiographic (ECG) evolution: Acute phase demonstrates prominent ST-segment elevations (typically in anterior precordial leads V2-V6 and limb leads I and aVL, characteristically without reciprocal ST-depression in inferior leads); evolves subacutely over 24-48 hours into widespread, striking, symmetric, deep T-wave inversions ('giant T-wave inversion' > 10 mm) and profound QT prolongation (predisposing to polymorphic VT/torsades de pointes); cardiac troponin biomarkers show disproportionately modest elevation relative to the extensive regional wall motion abnormality
radiological_manifestations: Catheterization & Left Ventriculography (Diagnostic Hallmark): Classic pathognomonic end-systolic appearance resembling a traditional Japanese narrow-necked octopus trap ('tako-tsubo'), displaying extensive akinesia, hypokinesia, or dyskinesia of the apical and mid-ventricular left ventricular segments with compensatory hyperkinesis of the basal segments, resulting in globular apical ballooning; Coronary Angiography reveals complete absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease, acute thrombus, or ruptured atheromatous plaque to account for the territory of dysfunction

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): Real-time visual confirmation of circumferential apical and mid-ventricular akinesia/ballooning extending well beyond the distribution of any single epicardial coronary artery; severe reduction of left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF typically 20-35% in acute phase); dynamic systolic anterior motion (SAM) of the mitral valve with LVOT obstruction and eccentric mitral regurgitation in up to 25% of cases; complete, spontaneous restoration and normalization of LV regional wall motion and ejection fraction documented on serial echocardiography within 4 to 8 weeks

Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CMR - Definitive Differential Diagnostic Tool): Cine SSFP sequences confirm the signature apical and mid-ventricular wall motion abnormalities; T2-weighted / T2-STIR sequences demonstrate diffuse, intense, transmural myocardial edema corresponding precisely to the dysfunctional apical and mid-ventricular myocardium; Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) is characteristically COMPLETELY ABSENT (or shows only faint, hazy, patchy non-ischemic interstitial enhancement), conclusively ruling out acute ischemic myocardial infarction (which displays dense subendocardial-to-transmural LGE) and acute viral myocarditis (which displays patchy mid-wall or subepicardial LGE)
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Endomyocardial Biopsy or Autopsy): Characteristic contraction band necrosis (hypercontracted, hyperdense, transverse eosinophilic bands composed of clumped sarcomeres alternating with disorganized myofilaments) caused by massive toxic supraphysiologic intramyocardial catecholamine surge and calcium overload; diffuse intracellular lipid accumulation and patchy myocyte vacuolization; sparse-to-moderate interstitial infiltration of mononuclear inflammatory cells (CD68+ macrophages and T-lymphocytes) without extensive polymorphonuclear neutrophilic infiltration and without true coagulation necrosis; normal epicardial coronary arteries devoid of acute thrombotic occlusion
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Archetypal neuro-cardiac stress disorder masquerading as STEMI, diagnosed by the pathognomonic 'octopus trap' apical ballooning on ventriculography/echocardiography in the absence of obstructive CAD, complete absence of late gadolinium enhancement on CMR, and hallmark catecholaminergic contraction band necrosis on histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Ventriculography diagnosis. Presentation is chest pain, not a visual finding.

excluded_topics.name: Uhl's Anomaly
synonyms: Congenital hypoplasia of right ventricular myocardium
clinical_manifestations: Neonatal/infantile right heart failure: Early, severe, and progressive right-sided congestive heart failure manifesting in infancy with intractable failure to thrive, tachypnea, prominent abdominal distension, ascites, and peripheral pitting edema

Profound central and peripheral cyanosis: Deep, progressive cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen therapy, driven by severely reduced pulmonary blood flow and an obligatory right-to-left shunt across a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect

Jugular venous examination: Severe, massive jugular venous distension with towering, giant 'v' waves and rapid 'y' descent resulting from severe functional tricuspid regurgitation and noncompliant right heart chambers; marked pulsatile hepatomegaly ('pulsatile liver')

Precordial physical examination: Strikingly quiet, adynamic, or completely 'silent' precordium over the right ventricle (conspicuous absence of the normal palpable right ventricular impulse despite massive cardiomegaly), distinguishing it clinically from hyperdynamic right ventricular enlargement

Cardiac auscultation: Soft, attenuated first heart sound (S1), widely split second heart sound (S2) with an inaudible or faint, delayed pulmonary closure sound (P2), prominent right-sided S3 and S4 gallop rhythms, and a soft, low-intensity holosystolic regurgitant murmur of secondary tricuspid insufficiency heard along the lower left sternal border
radiological_manifestations: Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE - Primary Diagnostic Modality): Massive, cavernous dilatation of the right ventricular chamber surrounded by an extraordinarily paper-thin, translucent, non-contractile right ventricular parietal free wall with global RV akinesia or paradoxical dyskinesia; normally positioned tricuspid valve leaflets with normal annular insertion (crucially distinguishing Uhl anomaly from Ebstein anomaly, which exhibits apical displacement of septal/posterior tricuspid leaflets); severe functional tricuspid regurgitation; preserved left ventricular muscular wall thickness and normal left ventricular ejection fraction; demonstration of right-to-left interatrial shunting through a stretched PFO or ASD

Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging (CMR - Modality of Choice for Tissue Characterization): Unsurpassed tomographic anatomical delineation confirming extreme attenuation of the entire right ventricular free wall to less than 1 mm (reduced to a membranous sheet consisting of opposed endocardium and epicardium devoid of trabeculae); massive right ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic volume indices with near-zero RV ejection fraction; critically differentiates Uhl anomaly from Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVC) by demonstrating COMPLETE ABSENCE of intramyocardial adipose tissue or fibrofatty infiltration within the thinned wall

Chest Radiography: Immense, dramatic cardiomegaly with a 'wall-to-wall' or box-shaped globular cardiac silhouette filling the thoracic cavity, accompanied by strikingly clear, hypoperfused, oligemic lung fields resulting from severely impaired right ventricular pulmonary forward output

Right Ventriculography (Catheterization): Massive, sluggish, adynamic right ventricular cavity with delayed clearance of contrast and complete absence of systolic wall contraction, functioning merely as a passive fibrous conduit for blood flow
pathology_manifestations: Gross Autopsy Pathology: Pathognomonic 'parchment heart' — the parietal free wall of the right ventricle is virtually devoid of muscular tissue and reduced to a translucent, paper-thin, shimmering membrane composed only of directly apposed visceral pericardium (epicardium) and endocardium; the right ventricular chamber is massively dilated, contrasting with a normally formed, fully muscular left ventricle and preserved interventricular septum; tricuspid and pulmonary valves are anatomically intact without downward leaflet displacement

Histopathology: Total or near-total selective absence (aplasia/severe hypoplasia) of right ventricular cardiac myocytes; microscopic examination of the right ventricular parietal wall demonstrates apposition of the endocardial elastic tissue and epicardial mesothelial fibroconnective layer with scattered fibrous collagen and total absence of muscle fibers; crucially, there is complete absence of the interstitial fibrofatty replacement and inflammatory adiposis characteristic of ARVC, and absence of endocardial elastosis
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Extreme structural congenital myocardial defect presenting with massive infantile right heart failure, giant 'v' waves, and a silent precordium, verified by the pathognomonic paper-thin 'parchment' RV wall on echocardiography/CMR, wall-to-wall cardiomegaly, and gross/microscopic total absence of RV myocytes without fibrofatty tissue.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Rare imaging/pathology diagnosis of a parchment right ventricle, without clinical photographs.

excluded_topics.name: Necrolytic Migratory Erythema
clinical_manifestations: Hallmark cyclic, dynamic rash that begins as erythematous macules or papules, evolving into polycyclic, annular, arcuate patches with central flaccid vesiculobullae that rupture, leaving oozing erosions, crusting, and post-inflammatory bronze/violaceous hyperpigmentation with peripheral scaling
Characteristic centrifugal migration and waxing-and-waning course over a 7- to 14-day cycle with spontaneous healing centrally while spreading peripherally
Distinct predilection for areas exposed to friction and trauma: perioral area, perineum, perianal region, buttocks, groin, genital region, and distal lower extremities

Prominent systemic features of the Glucagonoma Syndrome: painful, fiery-red, atrophic glossitis ('beefy-red' smooth tongue), angular cheilitis, marked unintentional weight loss, cachexia, normocytic normochromic anemia, severe deep vein thrombosis (DVT) / pulmonary embolism, and new-onset mild, nonketotic diabetes mellitus
Markedly elevated fasting plasma glucagon levels (frequently >500 to 1000 pg/mL; normal reference range <150 pg/mL)
radiological_manifestations: Multiphasic Contrast-Enhanced CT and MRI of Pancreas (Pancreatic Protocol): Identifies the primary glucagonoma, typically a large (>3 to 7 cm), hypervascular, well-circumscribed solid or cystic mass residing in the body or tail of the pancreas; exhibits intense contrast enhancement during late arterial/early pancreatic phase and rapid washout; reveals hypervascular liver metastases with rim enhancement and regional lymphadenopathy

Gallium-68 DOTATATE / DOTATOC Positron Emission Tomography (SSTR-PET/CT): Highly sensitive and specific imaging modality that exploits somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) overexpression on neuroendocrine tumors; demonstrates intense, focal radiotracer avidity within the pancreatic primary lesion and micro-metastatic disease in mesenteric lymph nodes and liver

Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS): Direct acoustic visualization of a hypoechoic, hypervascular mass in the pancreatic tail/body, providing real-time guidance for diagnostic fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or core biopsy

Venous Duplex Ultrasound and CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA): Identifies acute deep venous thrombosis (DVT) of lower extremities and pulmonary thromboembolism driven by glucagonoma-induced hypercoagulability
pathology_manifestations: Skin Punch Biopsy (Advancing Erythematous Edge): Pathognomonic superficial epidermal necrolysis: abrupt, sharp coagulative necrosis, pallor, and intracellular vacuolization (hydropic degeneration) confined to the upper third to half of the stratum spinosum and stratum granulosum, with sparing of the viable lower spinous and basal layers

Intraepidermal Blistering: Separation and clefting within the necrotic upper epidermis leading to subcorneal or intraepidermal splitting; overlying compact parakeratosis with aggregates of degenerated neutrophils forming subcorneal pustules (resembling Munro microabscesses)
Direct Immunofluorescence: Negative for immunoglobulins and complement, ruling out autoimmune blistering disorders

Pancreatic Tumor Histopathology: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm (NET) arranged in trabecular, insular, or gyriform patterns with uniform round nuclei, finely stippled 'salt-and-pepper' chromatin, and granular eosinophilic cytoplasm; strong immunohistochemical positivity for synaptophysin, chromogranin A, and glucagon
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Paraneoplastic endocrine dermatosis coupling migratory erosive annular plaques and painful glossitis with multiphasic abdominal CT/MRI and Ga-68 DOTATATE PET detection of a glucagonoma in the pancreatic body/tail.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Cutaneous manifestation of glucagonoma, already an endocrinology topic.

excluded_topics.name: Insulinoma
clinical_manifestations: Diagnostic Whipple Triad: (1) Classic symptoms of neuroglycopenia and sympathetic activation provoked by fasting or exertion; (2) Concomitantly documented profound hypoglycemia (venous plasma glucose <55 mg/dL [3.0 mmol/L]); and (3) Immediate, dramatic symptom resolution upon administration of exogenous oral or intravenous glucose

Acute Neuroglycopenic Manifestations: Progressive confusion, disorientation, bizarre behavioral changes, personality alterations, visual disturbances (diplopia, blurred vision), dysarthria, dizziness, stupor, grand mal generalized seizures, and unresponsiveness/hypoglycemic coma frequently misdiagnosed as epilepsy or transient ischemic attacks

Sympathoadrenal Autonomic Discharge Signs: Profuse cold diaphoresis, pallor, tachycardia, palpitations, wide pulse pressure, and fine resting and postural tremors occurring during acute hypoglycemic episodes

Compulsive Eating and Weight Gain: Marked, progressive weight gain and obesity developing as patients discover that continuous snacking and carbohydrate consumption prevents the onset of disabling neuroglycopenic spells
radiological_manifestations: Thin-Slice Multiphasic Pancreatic Contrast-Enhanced CT: Small (<2 cm; median 1.0–1.5 cm), well-circumscribed, round or oval solitary pancreatic mass demonstrating intense, early, homogeneous arterial phase contrast enhancement compared to surrounding hypoattenuating pancreatic parenchyma, with rapid isoattenuation on delayed venous phases

High-Resolution Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS): Premier localizing modality with >90–95% sensitivity: exquisitely circumscribed, homogeneous, round, hypoechoic nodule embedded within the pancreatic parenchyma, displaying intact smooth margins and prominent internal vascularity on Doppler interrogation

Dynamic Pancreatic Contrast MRI: Focal lesion displaying low to intermediate signal on T1-weighted images, bright hyperintensity on T2-weighted and diffusion-weighted (DWI) sequences with restricted diffusion, and avid early arterial contrast enhancement

68Ga-Exendin-4 PET/CT: Highly sensitive molecular imaging targeting the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R), which is expressed at extremely high density on benign insulinomas, providing definitive localization when CT and MRI are equivocal
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology: Solitary, well-circumscribed, encapsulated, fleshy, red-brown to yellow-tan nodule, typically measuring 1 to 2 cm, distributed evenly throughout the head, neck, body, or tail of the pancreas (>90% benign solitary tumors)

Histopathology: Well-differentiated neuroendocrine neoplasm (PanNET G1) composed of small, monomorphic, cuboidal cells with centrally placed round nuclei, fine 'salt-and-pepper' chromatin, and pale eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in trabecular, gyriform, nested, or solid architectural patterns; perivascular amyloid deposition composed of islet amyloid polypeptide (amylin) is frequently present

Immunohistochemistry: Strong, diffuse positivity for synaptophysin and chromogranin A, with specific intense cytoplasmic immunoreactivity for insulin and proinsulin; low Ki-67 proliferative index (<2%)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Premier cause of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia characterized by the classic Whipple triad, weight gain, and small (<2 cm) intensely arterial-enhancing pancreatic neuroendocrine nodule on multiphasic CT and endoscopic ultrasound.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Hypoglycemia syndrome. Whipple triad is not a visual finding.

excluded_topics.name: Nelson Syndrome
clinical_manifestations: Clinical history: Patient underwent bilateral adrenalectomy as treatment for refractory Cushing disease

Pathognomonic Cutaneous Sign: Deep, generalized, striking bronze, sepia, or slate-gray hyperpigmentation of the skin and mucous membranes, markedly accentuated in sun-exposed areas, palmar creases, axillae, knuckles, areolae, oral buccal mucosa, and surgical abdominal scars (caused by astronomical plasma ACTH and pro-opiomelanocortin [POMC] / alpha-MSH levels)

Aggressive Neuro-Ophthalmic Signs: Severe intractable headaches, progressive bitemporal hemianopsia (chiasmal compression), cranial nerve palsies (CN III, IV, VI due to cavernous sinus invasion), and hypopituitarism
radiological_manifestations: High-Resolution Contrast-Enhanced Sella and Brain MRI: Rapidly enlarging, aggressive, invasive pituitary macroadenoma (>10-20 mm) with heterogeneous enhancement, necrotic cystic degeneration, and suprasellar extension causing severe compression and superior displacement of the optic chiasm; invasive lateral parasellar extension into the cavernous sinuses with encasement of the intracavernous internal carotid arteries

Coronal and Sagittal Sella CT (Bone Window): Marked thinning, ballooning, and erosion of the sellar floor and dorsum sellae; destruction of the tuberculum sellae and sphenoid sinus invasion by the aggressive corticotroph tumor
pathology_manifestations: Corticotroph Pituitary Neuroendocrine Tumor (PitNET) Histopathology: Densely or sparsely granulated corticotroph adenoma composed of sheets of basophilic or chromophobic cells; intense cytoplasmic immunohistochemical positivity for ACTH and the line-defining transcription factor TPIT; high Ki-67 proliferation index (>3-5%) with frequent p53 nuclear positivity reflecting aggressive biological behavior; pathognomonic loss of negative glucocorticoid feedback following adrenalectomy
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Landmark endocrine entity where generalized bronze hyperpigmentation and bitemporal hemianopsia after adrenalectomy match aggressive invasive corticotroph macroadenoma on sella MRI.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Post-adrenalectomy pituitary manifestation of treated Cushing disease, not a primary image topic.

excluded_topics.name: Pituitary Apoplexy
clinical_manifestations: Hyperacute 'Thunderclap' Headache: Explosive, excruciating retro-orbital, frontal, or holocephalic headache of sudden onset (mimicking subarachnoid hemorrhage), accompanied by meningismus (nuchal rigidity, photophobia), intractable nausea, and projectile vomiting due to acute dural stretching and intrasellar pressure elevation

Acute Visual Chiasmal Syndrome: Sudden bilateral visual acuity reduction, severe bitemporal hemianopsia (documented on bedside visual field confrontation), constricted visual fields, or sudden monocular/binocular amaurosis resulting from upward hemorrhagic expansion compressing the optic chiasm and optic nerves

Pathognomonic Cranial Nerve Ophthalmoplegia: Unilateral or bilateral cranial nerve palsies due to lateral expansion into the cavernous sinuses, presenting with complete or partial oculomotor (CN III) palsy with ptosis, fixed dilated pupil, and 'down-and-out' globe position, trochlear (CN IV) palsy, and abducens (CN VI) palsy causing binocular diplopia and lateral rectus palsy

Acute Adrenal Crisis and Hemodynamic Collapse: Life-threatening acute secondary adrenal insufficiency presenting with sudden severe hypotension, hypothermia, cold pale extremities, hyponatremia, hypoglycemia, lethargy, confusion, and cardiovascular collapse secondary to acute corticotroph infarction and abrupt ACTH withdrawal
radiological_manifestations: High-Resolution Sellar and Pituitary MRI: Gold standard imaging showing an expansile, swollen, enlarged sellar and suprasellar mass with characteristic signal evolution based on hemorrhage age: acute phase (<48 hours) demonstrates T1 isointensity/hypointensity and T2 hypointensity; subacute phase (days 3–7) reveals pathognomonic striking peripheral or diffuse high signal intensity (hyperintensity) on T1-weighted images without contrast, forming a 'hyperintense crescent' or rim sign due to intracellular methemoglobin; reveals fluid-blood levels on T2-weighted sequences

Chiasmal Displacement and Cavernous Sinus Infiltration on Coronal MRI: Coronal T2-weighted MRI clearly demonstrates severe superior herniation of the necrotic mass draped over and stretching the optic chiasm ('chiasmal drape' sign) and lateral bulging into the cavernous sinus with encasement of the internal carotid artery

Emergency Non-Contrast Head CT: Visualizes an enlarged sella turcica containing a hyperdense intrasellar mass (representing acute hemorrhage), erosion or remodeling of the sellar floor, suprasellar mass effect with effacement of the optic chiasm and suprasellar cistern, and exclusion of aneurysm or subarachnoid hemorrhage
pathology_manifestations: Surgical Decompression Histopathology: Extensively necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue derived from a pituitary adenoma, showing confluent coagulative necrosis with ghost outlines of necrotic adenoma cells, extensive lake-like pools of extravasated erythrocytes, fibrin thrombi occluding intrasellar sinusoidal capillaries, and hemosiderin-laden macrophages bordering viable adenoma zones

Reticulin and Synaptophysin Stains: Reticulin stain demonstrates complete breakdown and loss of the normal pituitary acinar reticulin framework characteristic of an underlying macroadenoma; synaptophysin confirms neuroendocrine identity in residual non-necrotic adenoma cells
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Critical neuroendocrine emergency presenting with sudden thunderclap headache, bitemporal hemianopsia, CN III ophthalmoplegia with ptosis, and characteristic T1-hyperintense sellar hemorrhagic necrosis on pituitary MRI.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Acute hemorrhagic manifestation of a pituitary adenoma, not a separate disease.

excluded_topics.name: Primary Aldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome)
clinical_manifestations: Severe Refractory Hypertension: Marked, persistent, treatment-resistant hypertension requiring multiple antihypertensive medications (often ≥3 drugs including a diuretic), frequently accompanied by early Target Organ Damage including left ventricular hypertrophy, microalbuminuria, and hypertensive retinopathy (flame-shaped hemorrhages, cotton-wool spots, arteriovenous nicking)

Hypokalemic Neuromuscular Weakness and Paralysis: Episodic, severe proximal muscle weakness, profound generalized fatigue, muscle cramping, and intermittent flaccid quadriparesis resulting from severe potassium depletion (frequently unmasked by thiazide diuretics)

Hypokalemic Alkalotic Tetany: Spontaneous or provoked carpopedal spasms, perioral numbness, and paresthesias triggered by metabolic alkalosis-induced reductions in ionized calcium, with positive Trousseau and Chvostek signs

Nephrogenic Polyuria and Polydipsia: Nocturia, polyuria, and compensatory polydipsia caused by hypokalemia-induced renal concentrating defect (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus); absence of peripheral edema due to the renal 'aldosterone escape' phenomenon
radiological_manifestations: High-Resolution Adrenal Protocol Multiphasic CT: Small (typically 1–2 cm), solitary, well-circumscribed, round or oval, homogeneous unilateral adrenal cortical nodule characterized by low unenhanced attenuation (<10 Hounsfield Units [HU]) due to high intracytoplasmic lipid content; rapid contrast washout on delayed 15-minute scans with absolute percentage washout (APW) >60% and relative percentage washout (RPW) >40%, pathognomonic of benign cortical adenoma

Adrenal Chemical Shift MRI: Striking, diagnostic signal drop on out-of-phase (opposed-phase) T1-weighted gradient-echo images compared to in-phase images, confirming abundant intracellular lipid content and differentiating adenoma from lipid-poor adrenal metastases or carcinoma

Adrenal Vein Sampling (AVS) with Catheter Venography: Interventional radiologic gold standard demonstrating catheter positioning in bilateral adrenal veins and definitive lateralization of aldosterone secretion (>4:1 cortisol-corrected aldosterone ratio between dominant and non-dominant adrenal veins during ACTH infusion), establishing unilateral surgical curability
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology: Encapsulated, well-circumscribed, solitary adrenal cortical neoplasm featuring a characteristic vibrant, bright canary-yellow or golden-orange cut surface due to rich intracytoplasmic esterified cholesterol and lipid content, sharply demarcated from adjacent non-tumorous cortex

Histopathology: Neoplasm composed predominantly of large, lipid-rich clear cells resembling normal zona fasciculata cells with abundant vacuolated cytoplasm and small uniform round nuclei, intermixed with smaller hybrid cells resembling zona glomerulosa cells arranged in cords, nests, and clusters; lack of capsular/vascular invasion or atypical mitoses

Spironolactone Bodies: Eosinophilic, laminated, concentric, whorled intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies surrounded by a clear halo seen within adenoma cells following preoperative mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist (spironolactone) therapy, derived from hypertrophied smooth endoplasmic reticulum membranes

Immunohistochemistry: Intense, selective immunoreactivity for aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2) within adenoma cells, with complete suppression/negativity of CYP11B2 in the adjacent normal adrenal cortex
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Leading curable cause of endocrine hypertension presenting with refractory hypertension, hypokalemic tetany/paresis, lipid-rich adrenal CT nodule (<10 HU with >60% washout), and golden-yellow histology with spironolactone bodies.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Endocrine hypertension without clinical photographs. Same exclusion class as essential hypertension.

excluded_topics.name: Sheehan Syndrome
clinical_manifestations: Antecedent obstetric history of massive postpartum hemorrhage complicated by severe hypovolemic shock, requiring emergency blood transfusion or uterine packing/hysterectomy
Immediate Postpartum Hallmark Sign: Failure of lactation (agalactia) due to sudden prolactin deficiency, with failure of breast engorgement
Failure to resume menses (prolonged secondary postpartum amenorrhea) due to gonadotropin (LH/FSH) deficiency

Progressive Hypopituitarism Signs: Loss of axillary and pubic hair (secondary to adrenal and ovarian androgen failure); waxy, pale, alabaster cutaneous complexion with fine perioral and periorbital wrinkling; severe cold intolerance, extreme fatigue, apathy, weight loss, and postural hypotension
radiological_manifestations: High-Resolution Pituitary Contrast-Enhanced MRI: Acute phase demonstrates an enlarged, non-enhancing or peripherally ring-enhancing ischemic and necrotic pituitary gland with intrasellar non-hemorrhagic edema; chronic phase (months to years) reveals the pathognomonic complete "empty sella" (herniation of the suprasellar subarachnoid space and cerebrospinal fluid into the pituitary fossa, compressing and flattening the residual atrophic adenohypophysis into a paper-thin crescent <1-2 mm along the sellar floor)

Non-Contrast Sella CT (Bone Window): Normal dimensions of the bony sella turcica without expansile remodeling or bony destruction (critically distinguishing Sheehan empty sella from expansile cystic pituitary macroadenomas or craniopharyngiomas); confirms absence of intrasellar calcification
pathology_manifestations: Pituitary Histopathology: Massive ischemic coagulative necrosis of the anterior pituitary gland (adenohypophysis) with ghost-cell outlines of acinar structures, followed by macrophage resorption and dense fibrocollagenous scar tissue formation; posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis) is characteristically spared due to its independent direct arterial blood supply from the inferior hypophyseal arteries
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic obstetric-endocrine catastrophe where postpartum agalactia, loss of pubic/axillary hair, and alabaster skin correspond to pathognomonic MRI empty sella and pituitary coagulative necrosis.
