Plain Skeletal Radiography: Classic signs of active hypophosphatemic rickets including cupping, widening, fraying, and splaying of the metaphyses at the distal radius, ulna, and tibia; marked widening of the radiolucent physeal growth plates; diaphyseal cortical thickening and femoral/tibial bowing deformities
pathology_manifestations: Renal Biopsy Light Microscopy: Marked focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and focal global glomerulosclerosis; severe tubular atrophy and extensive interstitial fibrosis; prominent intra-tubular deposits and calcified casts (calcium phosphate and oxalate) within dilated tubular lumens

Electron Microscopy: Striking effacement, blunting, and loss of the proximal tubular brush-border microvilli; vacuolization and apical endocytic vesicular collapse in proximal tubular epithelial cells; podocyte foot process effacement; total absence of immune complex deposits

Molecular Genetics: Hemizygous pathogenic loss-of-function variants in CLCN5 (encoding the 2Cl-/H+ antiporter ClC-5, causing Dent-1 in ~65% of cases) or OCRL (encoding inositol polyphosphate 5-phosphatase, causing Dent-2 in ~15% of cases)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic X-linked proximal tubulopathy pairing low-molecular-weight proteinuria, rachitic skeletal bowing, and recurrent childhood stones with dense medullary nephrocalcinosis on CT and proximal brush-border collapse on electron microscopy.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Low-molecular-weight proteinuria tubulopathy without clinical photographs.

excluded_topics.name: Emphysematous Pyelonephritis
excluded_topics.subspecialty: Severe Renal Infections and Emergency Nephrology
clinical_manifestations: Severe, fulminant, septic presentation classically occurring in poorly controlled diabetic patients (or urinary tract obstruction): high swinging pyrexia, profound rigors, nausea, vomiting, lethargy, confusion, and refractory septic shock
Exquisite unilateral (or bilateral) costovertebral angle flank tenderness and palpable, tense, exquisitely painful flank fullness/mass

Subcutaneous crepitus / palpable emphysema: crackling palpable air within the subcutaneous tissue of the flank, costovertebral angle, or extending along the retroperitoneum onto the anterior abdominal wall (pathognomonic bedside physical hallmark when present)
Severe hemodynamic collapse: profound hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, mottled cool extremities, acute oliguria, and metabolic acidosis
radiological_manifestations:
Non-Contrast and Contrast Abdominal/Pelvic CT (Diagnostic Gold Standard & Staging): Pathognomonic presence of gas within the renal parenchyma, collecting system, and retroperitoneum, precisely staged by the Huang-Tseng CT Classification:
- Class 1: Gas localized exclusively to the collecting system (emphysematous pyelitis)
- Class 2: Gas confined within the renal parenchyma without extension into the extrarenal space
- Class 3A: Gas or purulent collection extending into the perinephric space (confined by Gerota's fascia)
- Class 3B: Gas or abscess extending into the pararenal space, retroperitoneum, or invading the psoas muscle
- Class 4: Bilateral emphysematous pyelonephritis or EPN in a solitary functional kidney

CT Imaging Morphology: Striated, streaky, mottled, or crescentic pockets of low attenuation (around -1000 Hounsfield Units, indistinguishable from atmospheric gas) replacing necrotizing renal parenchyma, surrounded by fluid collections, parenchymal edema, and extensive perinephric fat stranding
Plain Abdominal Radiography (KUB): Bubbly, mottled, crescent-shaped gas shadow outlining the renal contour or tracking along the psoas margin

Renal Ultrasound: Dirty acoustic shadowing with high-amplitude hyperechoic foci with reverberation artifacts ('ring-down' or 'comet-tail' artifacts) within the renal sinus and parenchyma, obscuring deeper structures
pathology_manifestations: Gross Nephrectomy / Resection: Severely congested, purulent, crepitant kidney containing ragged, gas-filled, necrotic cavities, yellowish-gray geographic abscesses, and extensive hemorrhagic cortical and medullary infarctions

Histopathology (Diagnostic Hallmark): Severe, diffuse, acute necrotizing inflammation with massive coagulative and liquefactive necrosis of glomeruli and tubules; extensive microvascular and interlobular arterial thrombosis, intra-arterial fibrin plugs, and dense neutrophilic infiltrates surrounded by gas vacuoles; marked disruption of tissue architecture with abundant colonies of Gram-negative gas-producing fermentative bacteria (Escherichia coli in ~70%, followed by Klebsiella pneumoniae and Proteus mirabilis)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Life-threatening fulminant renal infection pairing palpable flank crepitus and diabetic septic shock with pathognomonic parenchymal gas (-1000 HU) classified on abdominal CT (Huang-Tseng staging) and severe necrotizing parenchymal destruction with microthrombosis on pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: CT gas diagnosis of a severe infection, not a photographic disease.

excluded_topics.name: Encapsulating Peritoneal Sclerosis
clinical_manifestations: Develops in end-stage kidney disease patients exposed to long-term peritoneal dialysis (PD, typically >3-5 years) or triggered shortly after conversion to hemodialysis or following kidney transplantation

Physical examination: Palpable, firm, non-tender or tender irregular abdominal masses ('abdominal cocoon' sign) corresponding to conglomerated small bowel loops, accompanied by a tense, rigid, scaphoid or asymmetrically distended abdomen
Recurrent, intractable clinical small bowel obstruction: persistent postprandial nausea, bilious vomiting, colicky abdominal cramping pain, obstipation, and abdominal tympany

Profound cachexia and systemic malnutrition: severe involuntary weight loss, temporal muscle wasting, sunken eyes, hypoalbuminemia, and chronic low-grade systemic inflammatory state (elevated CRP and ESR)

Peritoneal dialysis ultrafiltration failure: progressive loss of osmotic water clearance across the peritoneal membrane, accompanied by cloudy, amber, or blood-stained peritoneal dialysis effluent (hemoperitoneum)
radiological_manifestations: Contrast-Enhanced Abdominal CT (Diagnostic Imaging Gold Standard): Pathognomonic 'abdominal cocoon' appearance—small bowel loops clustered, tethered, and conglomerated in the mid-abdomen enclosed within a dense, thickened fibrous mantle/capsule; diffuse peritoneal thickening (>2-3 mm) and extensive, sheet-like or curvilinear peritoneal calcification coating the visceral and parietal peritoneal surfaces, bowel serosa, and mesenteric leaves

Abdominal CT Secondary Findings: Loculated, fluid-filled ascites collections ('encysted ascites'), tethering and fixed angulation of small bowel loops with localized air-fluid levels and bowel wall thickening
Abdominal Plain Radiography: Clustered central gas-filled bowel loops encased by fine curvilinear, shell-like radiopaque calcifications outlining the peritoneal envelope

Abdominal Ultrasonography: Demonstration of small bowel loops grouped into a rigid, motionless conglomerate surrounded by a thick hyperechoic rind, exhibiting absent peristaltic motility ('tethered bowel sign')
pathology_manifestations: Gross Surgical Pathology: The visceral and parietal peritoneum is replaced by a massive, thick (up to several millimeters), dense, leathery, pearly-white or yellowish fibrocollagenous membrane ('cocoon') that encases and constricts the entire small intestine into a solid block

Peritoneal Biopsy Histopathology: Marked submesothelial fibrous expansion composed of densely packed, hyalinized collagen lamellae arranged parallel to the peritoneal surface; complete denudation/loss of the surface mesothelial monolayer; prominent proliferating submesothelial myofibroblasts expressing podoplanin (D2-40)

Vascular Pathology & Calcification: Severe obliterative vasculopathy in the peritoneal stroma characterized by concentric intimal fibroelastosis, smooth muscle medial hypertrophy, and marked luminal stenosis of microvessels; patchy foci of dystrophic calcification and metaplastic ossification with foreign-body giant cells
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Devastating late complication of peritoneal dialysis manifesting as progressive cachexia, palpable abdominal masses, and bowel obstruction, defined by pathognomonic CT 'abdominal cocoon' calcification and dense hyalinized submesothelial fibrosis on pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Dialysis complication rather than a primary visual disease.

excluded_topics.name: Fibromuscular Dysplasia
clinical_manifestations: Severe, accelerated, or treatment-resistant secondary hypertension in young to middle-aged females (typically 20-50 years of age) with absence of classic cardiovascular risk factors
Continuous or systolic epigastric or flank vascular bruit (high-pitched rushing murmur heard best with the diaphragm/bell along the upper abdominal quadrants or costovertebral angle)
Cervical / submandibular vascular bruits and pulsatile tinnitus ('whooshing' sound synchronized with cardiac systole) caused by concomitant internal carotid artery involvement

Cerebrovascular manifestations including transient ischemic attacks (TIAs), amaurosis fugax, or spontaneous cervical artery dissection presenting with Horner syndrome (unilateral ptosis, miosis, and facial anhidrosis)
Pulsatile headache and intracranial berry aneurysm rupture presenting with sudden 'thunderclap' headache and subarachnoid hemorrhage (present in ~7-10% of patients with multifocal FMD)
radiological_manifestations: Catheter Renal Digital Subtraction Angiography (Diagnostic Gold Standard) & CTA/MRA: Pathognomonic 'string-of-beads' appearance (medial fibroplasia in 80-85% of cases), characterized by alternating segments of post-stenotic aneurysmal ectasia that are wider than the normal lumen and concentric web-like fibrous stenotic rings, characteristically localized to the middle and distal two-thirds of the main renal artery and its intrarenal branch bifurcations (sparing the ostium and proximal 1 cm)

Catheter Angiography / CTA (Focal FMD Pattern): Smooth, concentric or eccentric tubular stenosis or solitary circumferential ring-like band ('hourglass' narrowing) typically seen in intimal or adventitial fibroplasia in children and young adults

Renal Duplex Ultrasonography: Marked focal systolic velocity acceleration with peak systolic velocity (PSV >180-200 cm/s), renal-to-aortic velocity ratio (RAR >3.5), and severe turbulent spectral broadening localized to the mid-to-distal renal artery; downstream intrarenal segmental branches demonstrate classic 'tardus-parvus' waveforms (prolonged acceleration time >0.07 s and flattened systolic peak)

Captopril Renal Scintigraphy (99mTc-MAG3): Marked unilateral deterioration in renal clearance, delayed time to maximum activity (Tmax >5 min), and persistent cortical tracer retention in the affected kidney 30-60 minutes following oral captopril challenge
pathology_manifestations: Medial Fibroplasia (80-85% of cases): Microscopic sections demonstrate alternating areas of marked medial thinning with loss of the internal elastic lamina (producing mural ectasias/aneurysms) and thick fibromuscular ridges composed of disorganized, hyperplastic collagen and smooth muscle bundles (producing the stenotic web rings)

Perimedial (Subadventitial) Fibroplasia (10-15%): Dense, homogenous, circumferential cuff of collagenous tissue deposited strictly within the outer half of the tunica media abutting the external elastic lamina, without true aneurysms

Intimal Fibroplasia (1-5%): Circumferential intimal proliferation of loose or dense collagenous tissue with reduplication and fragmentation of the internal elastic lamina, causing smooth focal concentric stenosis without lipid vacuolation or dystrophic calcification
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic non-atherosclerotic renovascular disease causing refractory hypertension in young females with audible bruits, the pathognomonic mid-distal 'string-of-beads' sign on renal CTA/angiography, and characteristic medial fibroplasia on vascular pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Angiographic string-of-beads finding without a disease-specific photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Medullary Sponge Kidney
clinical_manifestations: Recurrent episodes of acute renal colic and loin/flank pain secondary to spontaneous passage of calcium-based nephrolithiasis
Gross macroscopic or microscopic hematuria occurring intermittently throughout young adult life
Recurrent upper and lower urinary tract infections and acute pyelonephritis

Physical signs of associated hemihypertrophy: visible unilateral limb length or girth discrepancy, or facial asymmetry (seen in association with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome or isolated congenital hemihypertrophy in up to 25% of cases)
Impaired urinary concentrating ability manifesting as polyuria, polydipsia, and nocturia, frequently accompanied by distal renal tubular acidosis (incomplete type 1 dRTA)
radiological_manifestations: Multiphase CT Urography (CTU) / Intravenous Urography (Diagnostic Imaging Gold Standard): Pathognomonic 'bouquet of flowers', 'paintbrush', or 'spray of flowers' appearance produced by dense contrast medium pooling within clusters of ectatic and cystic dilated papillary collecting ducts of Bellini that radiate outward from the renal pyramids into the minor calyces on delayed excretory phase imaging

Non-contrast Abdominal CT / Plain Radiography (KUB): Medullary nephrocalcinosis characterized by multiple discrete, rounded, clustered radiopaque calcifications (composed of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate/apatite) confined strictly to the pyramids of one or both kidneys, corresponding precisely to the dilated ectatic ducts

Renal Ultrasound: Hyperechoic medullary pyramids ('bright pyramids' or 'echogenic pyramids') with posterior acoustic shadowing caused by clustered medullary microlithiasis, with preservation of normal cortical thickness and echogenicity
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology: Kidneys normal or slightly enlarged; cut section of medullary pyramids reveals a porous, spongy, swiss-cheese architecture characterized by innumerable small (1 to 7 mm), spherical or fusiform cystic dilatations of the terminal medullary collecting ducts communicating directly with the calyces

Histopathology: Markedly dilated papillary collecting ducts lined by cuboidal, column-like, or transitional-type epithelium, containing laminated calculi (microliths), calcium crystals, and desquamated cellular debris; surrounding medullary interstitium shows chronic lymphocytic inflammatory infiltration, patchy tubulointerstitial fibrosis, and tubular atrophy, while the outer renal cortex and glomeruli remain morphologically pristine
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic developmental medullary collecting duct disorder presenting with recurrent colic and hemihypertrophy, featuring the pathognomonic 'paintbrush' or 'bouquet of flowers' pooling on CT urography, clustered medullary nephrocalcinosis, and characteristic sponge-like dilated collecting ducts on pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Urographic diagnosis (paintbrush papillae) without clinical photographs.

excluded_topics.name: Nutcracker Syndrome
excluded_topics.subspecialty: Renovascular Disease and Urologic Compression Syndromes
synonyms: mesoaortic compression of the left renal vein
clinical_manifestations: Severe, postural or orthostatic left flank and loin pain radiating down to the posteromedial thigh and buttock, aggravated by upright posture, physical exertion, walking, or prolonged sitting, and dramatically relieved by the supine position

Recurrent episodes of gross, painless or colicky macroscopic hematuria (secondary to rupture of thin-walled, engorged calyceal and renal pelvic venous varices into the upper collecting system) or persistent microhematuria

Prominent left-sided scrotal varicocele ('bag of worms' appearance on inspection and palpation, expanding with Valsalva maneuver and persisting partially in supine position) in males due to high-pressure retrograde congestion into the left testicular vein
Pelvic congestion syndrome in females manifesting as prominent vulvar, perineal, and gluteal varicosities, chronic pelvic aching pain, dyspareunia, dysmenorrhea, and post-coital ache
Orthostatic proteinuria (marked postural proteinuria in the upright position that completely resolves upon lying flat) and chronic asthenic/slender body habitus with low body mass index
radiological_manifestations: Multidetector Contrast-Enhanced Abdominal CTA / MRA (Sagittal and Axial Views): Pathognomonic 'beak sign'—abrupt, knife-like tapering and compression of the left renal vein (LRV) as it traverses between the abdominal aorta and the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), with massive upstream distention and aneurysmal ballooning of the hilar LRV segment; ratio of hilar to aortomesenteric LRV diameter >4.0 to 5.0

Arterial Geometry on Sagittal CTA: Marked narrowing of the aortomesenteric (aorta-SMA) angle to <16°-22° (normal angle 45°-90°) and reduction of the aortomesenteric distance to <4-5 mm (normal 10-14 mm); demonstration of extensive retroperitoneal, left gonadal, and periureteral collateral venous networks

Renal Doppler Ultrasound: Peak systolic velocity (PSV) acceleration through the compressed aortomesenteric LRV segment (>100 cm/s), with a velocity ratio between the aortomesenteric and renal hilar segments >4.0-5.0

Left Renal Retrograde Venography with Pullback Manometry (Hemodynamic Gold Standard): Renocaval pressure gradient >=3 mmHg (normal <=1 mmHg) measured between the proximal left renal vein and the inferior vena cava, with direct fluoroscopic evidence of stagnant reflux into the dilated left gonadal vein and pelvic plexus
pathology_manifestations: Gross and Endoscopic Examination: Cystoscopy or flexible ureterorenoscopy demonstrates tortuous, engorged subepithelial venous varices within the renal pelvis, fornices, and calyces with active oozing of blood into the urine

Venous Histopathology: Resected collateral veins and venous segments reveal compensatory smooth muscle hypertrophy, medial fibrosis, subendothelial intimal hyperplasia, and focal fragmentation of elastic laminae secondary to chronic high-pressure venous hypertension

Renal Parenchymal Morphology: Light microscopy reveals marked vascular congestion of peritubular capillaries and medullary vasa recta with focal red cell extravasation into tubular lumens and the interstitium, while glomerular basement membranes and podocyte architecture remain intact
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic renovascular entrapment disorder in lean patients causing orthostatic flank pain, gross hematuria, and left varicocele/pelvic varices, confirmed by the pathognomonic CT 'beak sign' with aortomesenteric angle <16° and elevated renocaval pressure gradient >=3 mmHg.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Venous compression anatomy on Doppler/CT, not a photographic disease.

excluded_topics.name: Renal Papillary Necrosis
clinical_manifestations: Acute, excruciating renal colic (ureteral colic) mimicking acute nephrolithiasis, caused by the sloughing and downstream transit of necrotic papillary tissue through the ureter

Spontaneous passage of sloughed tissue fragments in the urine: gross visual identification of spongy, triangular, grayish-white or brownish necrotic papillary sloughs collected during urine straining (pathognomonic bedside macroscopic hallmark)
Gross macroscopic hematuria with dark, 'smoky', or tea-colored urine, often punctuated by sudden frank red blood and clots
High fever, shaking chills, and flank/costovertebral angle tenderness triggered by secondary obstructive pyelonephritis behind an impacted necrotic papilla

Predisposing systemic clinical contexts: analgesic abuse (analgesic nephropathy), sickle cell disease/trait, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, and severe chronic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) consumption (acronym POSTCARDS)
radiological_manifestations:
Multiphase CT Urography (CTU) / Retrograde Pyelography (Imaging Gold Standard):
- Pathognomonic 'Ring Shadow' sign: a detached, sloughed necrotic papilla sitting freely within the calyx, outlined circumferentially by dense contrast medium pooling around it
- 'Lobster-claw' sign / 'Ball-on-T' sign: contrast medium tracking into linear, excavated clefts or tracking tracts around the necrosing papillary core in the medullary pyramid
- Triangular, blunted, clubbed, or 'calyceal cup' cavities with complete absence of the normal sharp, concave calyceal fornices, representing empty papillary beds after complete sloughing
Plain Abdominal Radiography (KUB): Ring-like or triangular calcifications in the renal medulla/calyces representing secondary dystrophic calcification of retained, sloughed papillae
Renal Ultrasound: Sloughed, detached hyperechoic triangular papilla within the dilated collecting system, absence of normal medullary pyramids, and irregular, blunted calyces
pathology_manifestations: Gross Examination: Sharply demarcated, pale yellowish-white, gray, or brown, triangular or wedge-shaped necrotic lesions restricted to the apical inner two-thirds of the renal pyramids (renal papillae), with a distinct hyperemic, hemorrhagic border separating the necrotic papilla from viable medullary tissue

Histopathology (Diagnostic Hallmark): Coagulative necrosis of the papillary medullary pyramids and collecting ducts, characterized by total loss of nuclear staining while preserving pale, ghost-like cellular and tubular architecture; marked medullary ischemia caused by microvascular occlusion and capillary necrosis within the vasa recta spuria; demarcating zone showing dense polymorphonuclear neutrophilic infiltration, congestion, and subsequent detachment/cleavage from the underlying medulla leaving an excavated, denuded calyx
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic ischemic medullary catastrophe recognized at the bedside by acute colic with visible passage of triangular tissue sloughs in the urine, diagnosed by pathognomonic 'ring shadow' and 'lobster-claw' signs on CT urography, and coagulative papillary necrosis with vasa recta microthrombosis on pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Papillary complication of sickle cell disease, analgesic use, or diabetes.

excluded_topics.name: Von Hippel-Lindau Disease
clinical_manifestations: Retinal capillary hemangioblastomas (von Hippel angiomas): ophthalmoscopic funduscopic visualization of distinct orange-red, rounded capillary angiomas with markedly dilated, tortuous feeder arterioles and draining venules, commonly complicated by macular exudates, vitreous hemorrhage, and tractional retinal detachment

Neurological signs of central nervous system hemangioblastomas: cerebellar ataxia, gait instability, dysmetria, intentional tremor, and morning occipital headaches with projectile vomiting (obstructive hydrocephalus)
Bilateral, palpable, ballotable flank masses and abdominal fullness due to multicentric bilateral renal carcinomas and complex cystic kidney disease
Paroxysmal hypertension, severe episodic headaches, diaphoresis, and palpitations from functional adrenal or extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas / paragangliomas
Palpable epididymal nodule or fullness (papillary cystadenoma of the epididymis) in males, or broad ligament cystadenoma in females
radiological_manifestations: Multiphase Contrast-Enhanced Abdominal CT / MRI: Multiple, bilateral, synchronous, solid hypervascular renal cortical masses with rapid early arterial enhancement and washout (multicentric clear cell RCCs), interspersed among innumerable simple and complex thick-walled renal parenchymal cysts (Bosniak IIF-IV)
Adrenal CT / MRI / 123I-MIBG or 68Ga-DOTATATE PET: Bilateral hypervascular adrenal masses demonstrating intense T2 hyperintensity ('lightbulb sign' on MRI) confirming pheochromocytomas

Contrast-Enhanced Brain and Spine MRI: Pathognomonic vividly enhancing solid mural nodule nestled within the wall of a large, fluid-filled cystic lesion located within the cerebellum or cervical/thoracic spinal cord (CNS hemangioblastoma)

Pancreatic CT / MRI: Innumerable non-functioning pancreatic serous microcystic adenomas ('honeycomb' or 'sunburst' appearance with central calcified scar) and hypervascular pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (pNETs)
pathology_manifestations: Renal Histopathology: Multicentric, bilateral clear cell renal carcinomas composed of nests of lipid-rich clear polygonal cells with delicate capillary networks, intimately arising from the epithelial lining of precursor renal cysts lined by atypical clear cells with cytologic atypia; immunohistochemistry positive for CA-IX, PAX8, and CD10

Molecular Genetics / Pathophysiology: Germline loss-of-function mutation in the *VHL* tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 3p25, preventing ubiquitin-mediated proteasomal degradation of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF-1alpha and HIF-2alpha), resulting in unchecked transcriptional overdrive of angiogenic factors including VEGF, PDGF, and erythropoietin
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Premier autosomal dominant tumor syndrome pairing funduscopic retinal capillary hemangioblastomas and cerebellar cystic-mural nodule lesions with bilateral multicentric clear cell renal carcinomas and complex cysts on abdominal CT/MRI driven by VHL/HIF dysregulation.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Duplicate of the neurology von Hippel-Lindau topic.

excluded_topics.name: Balo Concentric Sclerosis
clinical_manifestations: Fulminant tumefactive neurologic deterioration: Rapidly progressive, stroke-like focal deficits (acute dense hemiplegia, expressive/receptive aphasia, hemianopia, hemisensory loss) evolving over days to weeks in young adults, closely masquerading as an acute cerebrovascular event or high-grade brain tumor
Intracranial hypertension syndrome: Severe intractable cephalalgia, projectile vomiting, papilledema, and obtundation resulting from massive vasogenic edema and mass effect of the tumefactive lesion
Neuropsychiatric collapse: Rapid cognitive decline, emotional incontinence, severe confusion, and delirium
Absence of peripheral inflammatory signs: Normal systemic inflammatory markers and afebrile presentation despite devastating focal CNS signs
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (Axial T2, FLAIR, T1, DWI, and T1+Gd): Pathognomonic alternating concentric rings or lamellar bands ('onion-bulb', 'tree-ring', or 'target' pattern) composed of alternating layers of demyelination (hyperintense on T2/FLAIR) and preserved or partially remyelinated white matter (isointense to hypointense on T2/FLAIR); Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) reveals concentric rings of restricted diffusion matching the active, expanding outer frontiers of demyelination; post-contrast T1 displays concentric alternating lamellar or open-ring rim enhancement; MR spectroscopy shows elevated choline, decreased NAA, and prominent lactate peaks
pathology_manifestations: Neuropathology / Stereotactic brain biopsy: Striking macroscopic and microscopic concentric alternating rings of total myelin loss and preserved/remyelinated myelin radiating outward from a central dilated venule; demyelinated zones show dense infiltration of foamy macrophages stuffed with luxol fast blue-positive myelin degradation products; relative preservation of axons within demyelinated bands; astrocytes at the leading edges express marked upregulation of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1alpha) and heat shock protein 70 (Hsp70), confirming hypoxia-like tissue preconditioning
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Legendary demyelinating condition with pseudo-tumoral stroke-like presentation, pathognomonic 'onion-bulb / tree-ring' concentric rings on brain MRI, and alternating bands of demyelination and spared myelin on tissue histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: MRI pattern / variant of demyelination, not an independent clinical-image disease.

excluded_topics.name: CLIPPERS Syndrome
synonyms: chronic lymphocytic inflammation with pontine perivascular enhancement responsive to steroids
clinical_manifestations: Subacute progressive pontocerebellar syndrome: Marked cerebellar gait and limb ataxia, scanning cerebellar dysarthria, diplopia, nystagmus, altered facial sensation (trigeminal sensory loss), and pseudobulbar laughing/crying
Exquisite glucocorticoid responsiveness: Dramatic, rapid clinical improvement and disappearance of symptoms within 24 to 48 hours of starting high-dose intravenous corticosteroid therapy

Rebound deterioration upon steroid withdrawal: Inevitable, prompt symptomatic and radiological relapse following corticosteroid tapering or discontinuation, necessitating long-term steroid-sparing immunosuppression
Absence of systemic inflammatory or neoplastic signs: Afebrile, no systemic organ involvement, negative antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (Axial and Coronal T1+Gd, T2/FLAIR): Pathognomonic punctate and curvilinear, nodular gadolinium enhancement centered within the pons, producing a distinctive 'peppering' or 'salt-and-pepper' appearance; lesions radiate into the brachium pontis (middle cerebellar peduncles), medulla, cerebellar hemispheres, and midbrain; individual lesions are typically small (<3 mm) without significant vasogenic edema or mass effect; T2/FLAIR shows faint, ill-defined punctate hyperintensities matching the enhancing lesions; repeat post-treatment MRI demonstrates striking, near-complete radiological resolution of enhancing punctate lesions following corticosteroid therapy
pathology_manifestations: Pontine or Brainstem Stereotactic Biopsy: Dense, marked perivascular and parenchymal infiltration composed predominantly of mature CD3+ and CD4+ T lymphocytes and CD68+ histiocytes forming perivenular cuffs around small blood vessels in the pons and cerebellar white matter; absence of necrotizing vasculitis, absence of non-caseating granulomas, absence of Reed-Sternberg cells or clonal B-cell populations, and absence of viral or fungal inclusions
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Unique neuroinflammatory syndrome characterized by pontocerebellar ataxia, pathognomonic 'peppering / salt-and-pepper' pontine gadolinium enhancement on MRI with rapid steroid responsiveness, and perivascular CD4+ T-cell lymphocytic cuffs on biopsy.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Punctate MRI pattern with brainstem signs, without a photographic phenotype.

excluded_topics.name: Central Pontine Myelinolysis
clinical_manifestations: Biphasic neurologic deterioration: Initial clinical recovery from severe hyponatremic encephalopathy followed 2 to 7 days later by acute, devastating neurologic decline after rapid electrolyte correction (>10-12 mEq/L in 24 hours)
Locked-in syndrome: Progression to complete anarthria (mutism) and spastic quadriplegia, with preservation of vertical eye movements and voluntary eyelid blinking as the sole means of communication
Pseudobulbar palsy: Severe dysarthria, dysphagia, emotional lability, and loss of gag reflex from corticobulbar tract demyelination
Extrapontine myelinolysis manifestations: Parkinsonian rigidity, resting tremor, painful dystonia, choreoathetosis, and catatonia resulting from basal ganglia involvement
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (Axial and Sagittal T2, FLAIR, DWI, and T1+Gd): Pathognomonic symmetrical, sharply demarcated, trident-shaped, bat-wing, or triangular T2/FLAIR hyperintensity centered in the basis pontis, with hallmark, classic sparing of the ventrolateral pons, tegmentum, and descending corticospinal tracts; early Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) reveals prominent restricted diffusion (high DWI, low ADC) in the central pons appearing days before T2 signal abnormalities; T1-weighted images demonstrate symmetrical hypointensity without abnormal gadolinium enhancement or mass effect; Extrapontine Myelinolysis (EPM) demonstrates symmetrical T2 hyperintensity in the bilateral caudate, putamen, and thalamus
pathology_manifestations: Neuropathology / Autopsy: Macroscopically well-demarcated, symmetrical, soft, brownish triangular area of demyelination in the central basis pontis; microscopic examination reveals extensive loss of myelin sheaths and destruction of oligodendrocytes with remarkable, pristine preservation of axis cylinders (axons) and neuronal cell bodies; dense infiltration of foamy lipid-laden CD68+ macrophages engulfing myelin debris; notable absence of perivascular lymphocytic cuffs or primary vascular inflammation (non-inflammatory osmotic oligodendrocyte apoptosis)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic osmotic demyelinating catastrophe with dramatic locked-in physical syndrome, pathognomonic bat-wing/trident-shaped basis pontis T2 hyperintensity sparing the periphery on MRI, and selective myelinolysis with spared axons on histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: MRI diagnosis of an osmotic demyelination syndrome. No clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy
clinical_manifestations: Severe migraine with prolonged aura: Onset of atypical migraines with hemiplegic, visual, sensory, or basilar aura starting in the third decade of life (mean age ~25-30 years)

Recurrent subcortical ischemic strokes: Repeated transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) and lacunar strokes occurring in young to middle-aged adults (40s-50s) in the complete absence of classical cardiovascular risk factors (hypertension, smoking, hyperlipidemia)
Progressive vascular cognitive impairment: Stepwise cognitive decline, executive dysfunction, apathy, pseudobulbar palsy, and severe subcortical vascular dementia
Severe mood and psychiatric disturbances: Bipolar-like mood swings, recurrent major depression, and severe personality changes in up to 30-40% of patients
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (Axial T2, FLAIR, T1, and SWI): Pathognomonic, highly specific (~90-95%) symmetrical T2/FLAIR hyperintensity involving the anterior temporal poles (O'Sullivan sign); symmetric confluent hyperintensities involving the external capsules and corpus callosum; diffuse, confluent periventricular and deep white matter hyperintensities sparing subcortical U-fibers; multiple small, punched-out cavitary lacunar infarcts in the basal ganglia, internal capsules, and pons; Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI) or T2* GRE reveals multiple microbleeds in the thalamus, basal ganglia, and brainstem
pathology_manifestations: Skin Punch Biopsy and Neuropathology: Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) of dermal arterioles reveals the pathognomonic ultrastructural hallmark: dense, osmiophilic, periodic granular deposits designated Granular Osmiophilic Material (GOM) located within the basement membrane directly adjacent to vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs); immunohistochemistry shows accumulation of the extracellular domain of NOTCH3 (NOTCH3-ECD); vascular pathology shows non-atherosclerotic, non-amyloid progressive VSMC apoptosis, concentric adventitial fibrosis, and severe luminal stenosis of small penetrating cerebral and dermal arteries; confirmed by NOTCH3 gene mutations involving cysteine residues on chromosome 19p13.2
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Hereditary small-vessel neurovascular syndrome with early severe migraine/subcortical strokes, pathognomonic anterior temporal pole and external capsule MRI hyperintensities (O'Sullivan sign), and diagnostic vascular granular osmiophilic material (GOM) on skin biopsy.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: MRI leukoencephalopathy and lacunar disease. No disease-specific clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Neurosarcoidosis
clinical_manifestations: Cranial neuropathy: Peripheral facial nerve palsy (cranial nerve VII), frequently bilateral, alternating, or recurrent; Heerfordt syndrome triad of facial nerve palsy, parotid gland enlargement, anterior uveitis, and low-grade fever
Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction: Central diabetes insipidus (polydipsia, polyuria), hyperprolactinemia, panhypopituitarism, amenorrhea, and thermal dysregulation due to infundibular infiltration

Visual failure and optic neuropathy: Papilledema from elevated intracranial pressure, compressive optic neuropathy with optic atrophy, granulomatous uveitis with mutton-fat keratic precipitates, and retinal periphlebitis (candle-wax drippings / tache de bougie)
Cutaneous sarcoid lesions: Lupus pernio (violaceous, indurated, telangiectatic plaques on the nose, cheeks, and earlobes), erythema nodosum, and scar infiltration by granulomas
radiological_manifestations: Brain Contrast-Enhanced MRI: Pathognomonic diffuse or nodular leptomeningeal enhancement coating the basal cisterns, perichiasmatic region, infundibular stalk, and folia; dural-based mass-like enhancing lesions mimicking meningiomas ('sarcoid dural plaquing'); hypothalamic-pituitary axis thickening and avid contrast enhancement; parenchymal non-caseating granulomatous nodules with surrounding T2/FLAIR vasogenic edema

Spine MRI: Longitudinally extensive intramedullary hyperintense lesions with nodular subpial surface gadolinium enhancement producing the pathognomonic 'trident sign' on post-contrast axial T1 sequences; focal cord swelling and leptomeningeal nodularity

Chest Radiography and HRCT: Symmetrical bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (BHL) and right paratracheal lymphadenopathy (Garland triad / 1-2-3 sign); perilymphatic micronodules along bronchovascular bundles and subpleural fissures; Galaxy sign (confluent central granulomas surrounded by tiny satellite nodules)
18F-FDG PET/CT: Hypermetabolic uptake in basal leptomeninges, dural masses, mediastinal/hilar lymph nodes, and cardiac myocardium
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Brain, meningeal, or nodal biopsy): Non-caseating, well-circumscribed epithelioid cell granulomas composed of tightly clustered epithelioid histiocytes, Langhans-type and foreign-body multinucleated giant cells, rimmed by a sparse outer cuff of CD4+ T lymphocytes and fibroblasts; giant cells frequently contain Schaumann bodies (concentric laminated basophilic calcifications) or asteroid bodies (stellate eosinophilic inclusions); special stains (GMS, PAS, Ziehl-Neelsen) strictly negative for fungi and acid-fast bacilli
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic granulomatous neuroinflammatory disorder featuring facial palsy/Heerfordt syndrome, lupus pernio, pathognomonic basal leptomeningeal nodular enhancement and spinal 'trident sign' on MRI, and non-caseating granuloma pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Neurologic manifestation of sarcoidosis, already a pulmonology topic.

excluded_topics.name: Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy
clinical_manifestations: Subacute progressive focal neurologic deficits: Rapidly accumulating hemiparesis, limb and ideomotor apraxia, ataxia, and aphasia over weeks in immunocompromised hosts (HIV/AIDS with CD4 <200, natalizumab/efalizumab/rituximab therapy for MS or Crohn, hematologic malignancies)
Visual pathway defects: Homonymous hemianopia, visual agnosia, and cortical blindness due to occipital lobe white matter involvement, with preserved pupillary light reflexes
Cognitive and behavioral decline: Progressive dementia, personality blunting, abulia, and confusion progressing without fever or signs of meningismus
Absence of headache or intracranial hypertension: Normal intracranial pressure without papilledema, reflecting the non-mass-occupying nature of demyelinating necrosis
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (Axial T2, FLAIR, T1, DWI, and T1+Gd): Pathognomonic scalloped subcortical white matter lesions that characteristically involve the subcortical arcuate U-fibers, yielding a razor-sharp demarcation at the cortical gray-white junction and a fuzzy, ill-defined margin toward deep white matter; lesions appear intensely hyperintense on T2/FLAIR and deeply hypointense ('punched-out') on T1-weighted images; Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI) shows a rim of bright restricted diffusion along the active advancing border; lack of mass effect and lack of contrast enhancement in classic PML (vivid perilesional enhancement signals Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome [PML-IRIS])
pathology_manifestations: Neuropathology / Stereotactic Brain Biopsy: Diagnostic histopathologic triad: 1) Multifocal, confluent zones of demyelination with relative axonal preservation; 2) Markedly enlarged oligodendrocytes with ground-glass, amphophilic to basophilic intranuclear viral inclusions situated at the borders of demyelinating lesions; 3) Giant, bizarre, pleomorphic multinucleated astrocytes with hyperchromatic, monstrous, lobulated nuclei mimicking neoplastic cells; immunohistochemistry for SV40/JCV VP1 capsid protein strongly highlights infected oligodendrocytic nuclei; electron microscopy displays paracrystalline arrays of 40-nm icosahedral JC polyomavirus particles
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Severe opportunistic demyelinating illness presenting with subcortical focal deficits, pathognomonic U-fiber-scalloped non-enhancing MRI lesions with advancing DWI rim, and diagnostic enlarged inclusion-bearing oligodendrocytes with bizarre giant astrocytes.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: MRI and CSF diagnosis. Clinical deficits are not photographable disease findings.

excluded_topics.name: Superficial Siderosis of the Central Nervous System
synonyms: superficial hemosiderosis of the central nervous system
clinical_manifestations: Sensorineural hearing loss: Progressive, insidious, bilateral, symmetrical sensorineural deafness that is almost universal (>95% of patients), typically beginning with high-frequency loss before progressing to profound deafness, due to vulnerable long glial-Schwann cell transitional zones of the eighth cranial nerve (vestibulocochlear nerve) bathed in subarachnoid blood

Cerebellar ataxia: Progressive gait and truncal ataxia, dysmetria, intention tremor, scanning dysarthria, and past-pointing resulting from preferential hemosiderin toxicity, oxidative stress, and extensive degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells

Pyramidal corticospinal myelopathy: Progressive spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign), and lower extremity stiffness caused by chronic hemosiderin encasement and axonal degeneration of the superficial descending corticospinal tracts in the spinal cord
Anosmia: Early loss of the sense of smell resulting from toxic iron accumulation along the olfactory bulbs and tracts
Neurogenic bladder and bowel dysfunction: Urgency, frequency, and urge incontinence developing secondary to chronic spinal cord involvement and spastic neurogenic bladder
radiological_manifestations: Brain MRI (T2-weighted, T2* Gradient Echo, and SWI): Pathognomonic, continuous, linear low-signal (black) hypointense rim 'capping' and coating the leptomeningeal surface of the cerebellar folia, brainstem (midbrain, pons, medulla), sylvian fissures, and cranial nerves (especially CN VIII); marked pronounced cerebellar atrophy (predominantly vermian and hemispheric folial volume loss); dramatic blooming artifact on T2* and SWI due to extensive paramagnetic hemosiderin iron deposition

Spine MRI (T2 and Gradient Echo): Continuous linear hypointense black coating encasing the entire surface of the spinal cord (pial hemosiderosis); spinal cord atrophy; T2-weighted MRI or MR myelography reveals the underlying chronic dural source of subarachnoid bleeding, such as a ventral dural tear, extradural fluid collection, pseudomeningocele, or dural defect (frequently at the cervicothoracic or thoracolumbar junction)

CT Myelography / Digital Subtraction Myelography: Dynamic myelography accurately pinpoints the exact site of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leakage and chronic dural breach/tear causing recurrent occult microhemorrhage into the subarachnoid space
pathology_manifestations: Gross and Microscopic Neuropathology: Striking dark-brown, rusty or black discoloration coating the surface of the cerebellum, cerebellar folia, brainstem, spinal cord, and leptomeninges; massive iron (ferritin and hemosiderin) deposition in the subpial Bergmann glia, microglia, and astrocytes of the superficial central nervous system, staining intensely blue with Prussian blue (Perls stain); profound, selective loss of cerebellar Purkinje cells with replacement by Bergmann astrogliosis; chronic axonal loss, myelin degeneration, and dense subpial fibrous gliosis; microscopic iron pigment granules packed within macrophages and free in subpial extracellular space
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic disabling neurological syndrome defined by the clinical triad of bilateral sensorineural deafness, cerebellar ataxia, and spastic myelopathy, matched with unmistakable MRI T2/SWI linear black hypointense rim coating the cerebellar folia and brainstem, driven by chronic occult dural CSF leaks.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: MRI hemosiderin staining. Hearing loss and ataxia are not photographic.

excluded_topics.name: Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion
clinical_manifestations: Second most frequent retinal vascular disease (surpassed only by diabetic retinopathy); typically occurs in adults over 60 years old in the setting of chronic systemic arterial hypertension, arteriosclerosis, and diabetes mellitus

Patients present with sudden, painless, unilateral reduction of central visual acuity (when the macula is involved) or an abrupt sectoral visual field defect corresponding geometrically to the affected retinal quadrant
Predilection for the superotemporal quadrant (~60% of cases), followed by inferotemporal (~30%), with rare nasal involvement

Pathognomonic Funduscopic Hallmark: Sectoral, wedge-shaped or fan-shaped distribution of dense intraretinal hemorrhages (superficial flame-shaped and deep dot-blot hemorrhages), localized retinal edema, and cotton-wool spots strictly confined to the retinal area drained by the occluded venous tributary

Pathognomonic Arteriovenous (A/V) Crossing Site: The apex of the hemorrhagic wedge points directly to an arteriovenous crossing site displaying pronounced arteriolar sclerosis and arteriolovenular crossing compression (Gunn sign / Salus sign), where the rigid arteriole compresses the underlying tributary venule

Chronic manifestations: Retinal collaterals ('shunt vessels') developing across the horizontal raphe to bypass the obstruction (dilated, tortuous venules connecting the obstructed sector to unobstructed venous beds), circinate hard exudate rings, and neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) or of the disc (NVD) predisposing to vitreous hemorrhage
radiological_manifestations: Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Pathognomonic sectoral demarcation: delayed venous transit and filling strictly distal to the arteriovenous crossing; intense blockage of choroidal background fluorescence by intraretinal hemorrhages; distinct wedge-shaped zones of capillary non-perfusion (ischemic BRVO defined by ≥ 5 disc diameters of capillary non-perfusion); late diffuse hyperfluorescent dye leakage from incompetent capillaries and macular edema; collateral vessels demonstrate slow laminar flow without late leakage, whereas neovascular fronds (NVE) display rapid profuse blooming leakage

Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography (SD-OCT): Highly specific for identifying and tracking sector-limited Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): exhibits hypo-reflective intraretinal fluid pockets in the Henle layer and outer plexiform layer strictly bounded by the horizontal raphe, subretinal fluid accumulation, hyperreflective intraretinal lipid foci, and outer retinal disruption (ellipsoid zone attenuation)

Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA): Non-invasively visualizes focal microvascular dropout, telangiectatic terminal capillaries, and foveal capillary ring breakdown in both superficial and deep capillary plexuses within the involved sector

Humphrey Visual Field (HVF): Dense, sharply demarcated sectoral altitudinal or quadrantanopic visual field defect that strictly respects the horizontal meridian corresponding to the anatomically obstructed sector
pathology_manifestations: Microvascular Histopathology: Thrombotic occlusion and endothelial proliferation of a branch retinal vein at the exact site of crossing beneath a sclerotic retinal arteriole; within the shared periadventitial connective tissue sheath, arterial sclerosis causes mechanical narrowing, hemodynamic turbulence, and shear-stress endothelial denudation of the underlying thin-walled venule

Tissue Architecture Changes: Massive extravasation of red blood cells and proteinaceous transudate into the nerve fiber, ganglion cell, and inner nuclear layers within the affected quadrant; swelling and fragmentation of unmyelinated axons (cytoid bodies) forming cotton-wool spots; localized VEGF upregulation in ischemic Muller and ganglion cells; chronic recanalization of the venous lumen with mural fibromuscular thickening
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: High-yield retinal vascular disorder featuring a pathognomonic wedge-shaped hemorrhagic sector originating at an arteriovenous nicking site, quadrant-restricted CME on SD-OCT, and sector-limited capillary non-perfusion on FA.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Retinal vascular event, usually a manifestation of systemic vascular disease rather than a disease entity.

excluded_topics.name: Brown Syndrome
synonyms: Brown superior oblique tendon sheath syndrome
clinical_manifestations: Pathognomonic ocular motility restriction: Severe limitation or complete inability to elevate the adducted eye, while elevation in abduction is completely normal or only minimally reduced
Normal ocular alignment in primary gaze, or slight hypotropia of the affected eye; divergence (V-pattern) on upgaze
Characteristic chin-up head posture (compensatory elevation of chin) and slight head tilt to maintain binocular single vision
Widening of the palpebral fissure on attempted adduction (contrasting with Duane syndrome narrowing); audible or palpable 'click' at the superomedial orbital rim during forced elevation
Forced Duction Testing (Pathognomonic Bedside/Surgical Maneuver): Demonstrates profound mechanical restriction to passive elevation of the globe when rotated into adduction
radiological_manifestations: High-Resolution Orbit MRI (T1, T2, and 3D CISS/FIESTA with surface coils): In acquired Brown syndrome, focal thickening, enlargement, and hyperintense T2 signal within the superior oblique tendon/trochlear complex reflecting inflammatory tenosynovitis, with post-contrast enhancement of the trochlea and tendon sheath

Congenital Brown Syndrome Imaging: Demonstrates a short, inextensible, taut superior oblique tendon complex, abnormal fibrous bands tethering the tendon to the orbital wall, or cysts of the tendon sheath restricting passage through the cartilaginous trochlear pulley
pathology_manifestations: Tenosynovial Histopathology: Dense fibrous thickening, chronic lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, and synovial hyperplasia of the superior oblique tendon sheath; focal nodular fibrosis or stenosing tenosynovitis preventing smooth translation through the trochlear ring
Absence of primary muscular dystrophy or denervation of extraocular muscles
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic mechanical strabismus motility defect (limited elevation in adduction) with positive forced duction test, high-resolution orbital MRI trochlear thickening, and trochlear tenosynovial pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Restricted-motility finding, not a disease with a gallery of clinical images.

excluded_topics.name: Central Retinal Artery Occlusion
clinical_manifestations: Sudden, catastrophic, painless, monocular complete or near-complete visual loss (typically counting fingers or light perception) occurring over seconds
Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) in the affected eye
Pathognomonic Funduscopic Appearance: Diffuse milky-white, opaque, ischemic clouding/edema of the posterior retina (especially nerve fiber layer and ganglion cell layer)

Classic 'Cherry-Red Spot' at the foveola: Because the foveola lacks inner retinal layers and is nourished by the underlying healthy choriocapillaris, the bright red choroidal vascular bed shines conspicuously through the attenuated fovea against the surrounding opaque white retina
'Boxcarring' or cattle-trucking: Segmentation and fragmentation of blood columns within attenuated retinal arterioles; visible Hollenhorst plaques (refractile cholesterol crystal at bifurcations)
radiological_manifestations: Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Dramatic prolongation of retinal arm-to-retina circulation time (>20-30 seconds), absent or severely sluggish retinal arteriolar filling with delayed arteriovenous transit time; choroidal circulation fills normally (differentiating from ophthalmic artery occlusion)

Spectral-Domain OCT (SD-OCT): Acute phase demonstrates dramatic hyperreflectivity and intracellular edema/thickening of the inner retinal layers (nerve fiber, ganglion cell, inner plexiform, and inner nuclear layers), with corresponding optical shadowing of underlying photoreceptor layers; chronic phase demonstrates profound thinning and complete atrophy of inner retinal layers
Carotid Duplex Ultrasound and CT/MR Angiography: High prevalence of ipsilateral internal carotid artery stenosis/ulcerated atheromatous plaque as the embolic source
pathology_manifestations: Retinal Histopathology: Acute ischemic coagulative necrosis and intracellular cytotoxic edema of retinal ganglion cells and axonal swellings (cytoid bodies); chronic stage shows complete disappearance of the ganglion cell layer and severe thinning of the retinal nerve fiber layer, while photoreceptor and RPE layers remain structurally preserved
Vascular Histology: Embolic occlusion of the central retinal artery lumen within the retrobulbar optic nerve or lamina cribrosa
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic ophthalmic medical emergency with unforgettable funduscopic 'cherry-red spot' on opaque white retina, boxcarring arterioles, and inner retinal hyperreflectivity on OCT.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Ophthalmic vascular event / manifestation, not a disease-level topic.

excluded_topics.name: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion
clinical_manifestations: Major sight-threatening retinal vascular disease, predominantly affecting patients older than 50 years with systemic vascular risk factors (hypertension, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypercoagulable states, primary open-angle glaucoma, and vasculitis)

Patients present with sudden, painless, unilateral vision loss, ranging from mild blurring in non-ischemic CRVO to catastrophic drop in visual acuity (finger counting or hand motions) in ischemic CRVO
Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD / Marcus Gunn pupil) is prominently present in ischemic CRVO, serving as an essential bedside prognostic differentiator

Pathognomonic Funduscopic Hallmark: Classic 'Blood-and-Thunder' fundus: massive, extensive intraretinal hemorrhages involving all four retinal quadrants, featuring both superficial flame-shaped hemorrhages in the retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) and deep round blot hemorrhages in the inner nuclear layer

Associated Ocular Signs: Markedly engorged, tortuous, dark-purple retinal veins; diffuse cotton-wool spots (microinfarctions of the axonal nerve fiber layer); severe hyperemic optic disc swelling with blurred margins; macular edema; late development of anterior segment rubeosis iridis and neovascular glaucoma (traditionally termed '90-day glaucoma' in untreated ischemic CRVO)
radiological_manifestations: Fluorescein Angiography (FA): Gold-standard vascular diagnostic imaging; demonstrates markedly delayed arm-to-retina transit time and prolonged retinal venous filling (>20-30 seconds); extensive hypofluorescence from widespread masking/blockage by dense intraretinal hemorrhages; capillary non-perfusion defining ischemia (ischemic CRVO defined by ≥ 10 disc areas of retinal capillary non-perfusion on widefield FA); late profuse dye leakage from dilated optic disc capillaries, retinal venules, and macular capillary bed

Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography (SD-OCT): Highly sensitive for quantifying Cystoid Macular Edema (CME): shows extensive hypo-reflective intraretinal fluid-filled cystic cavities within the outer plexiform and inner nuclear layers, subfoveal neurosensory retinal detachment (subretinal fluid), hyperreflective intraretinal dots (lipid exudates/inflammatory cells), and disorganization of retinal inner layers (DRIL) correlating with poor functional visual recovery

Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA): Non-invasively visualizes profound capillary drop-out, foveal avascular zone (FAZ) enlargement and irregularity, and flow voids within both the superficial and deep capillary plexuses without dye obscuration from hemorrhages

Color Doppler Ultrasonography of Central Retinal Vessels: Demonstrates markedly reduced peak systolic velocity (PSV) and end-diastolic velocity (EDV) within the central retinal vein at the lamina cribrosa, with an elevated vascular pulsatility index
pathology_manifestations: Thrombotic Histopathology: Fresh, organizing, or recanalized luminal thrombus within the central retinal vein located at or just posterior to the level of the lamina cribrosa (where the central retinal artery and vein share a common rigid fibrous adventitial sheath and venous lumen is anatomically narrowed)

Vascular and Endothelial Changes: Endothelial cell hyperplasia, subendothelial lipohyalinosis, and mechanical compression of the vein by an arteriosclerotic central retinal artery; severe venous wall phlebosclerosis

Retinal Parenchymal Histology: Massive intraretinal erythrocyte extravasation spanning all retinal layers from the nerve fiber layer down to the photoreceptor layer; severe intracellular and extracellular edema; cytoid bodies (axoplasmic stasis in swollen ganglion cell axons); dramatic hypoxia-induced upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) driving microvascular permeability and subsequent pre-retinal and iridal fibrovascular proliferation (neovascularization)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Archetypal retinal vascular emergency presenting with the unforgettable 'blood-and-thunder' fundus across all four quadrants, FA venous stasis, SD-OCT cystoid macular edema, and lamina cribrosa venous thrombosis.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Retinal vascular event / manifestation, not a disease-level topic.

excluded_topics.name: Horner Syndrome
synonyms: apical Pancoast tumor syndrome with Horner
clinical_manifestations: Neuro-ophthalmic syndrome caused by interruption of the three-neuron oculosympathetic pathway anywhere along its trajectory from the posterolateral hypothalamus to the ocular globe

Pathognomonic Bedside Clinical Triad: 1) Ipsilateral Miosis: Pupillary constriction of the affected eye due to unopposed parasympathetic sphincter tone, resulting in anisocoria that is significantly more pronounced in darkness (due to impaired dilation) with demonstrable 'dilation lag' when lights are turned off; 2) Partial Ptosis: Mild (1-2 mm) drooping of the upper eyelid due to sympathetic denervation of the involuntary superior tarsal muscle of Müller; 3) 'Upside-Down' or Inverse Ptosis: Elevation of the lower eyelid margin due to paralysis of the inferior tarsal muscle, causing an overall narrowing of the palpebral fissure that imparts the false appearance of enophthalmos ('apparent enophthalmos')

Anhidrosis: Loss of sweating and flushing over the ipsilateral hemiface, neck, and upper chest (seen in first-order central and second-order preganglionic lesions; spared in third-order postganglionic lesions because sudomotor fibers to the face branch off along the external carotid artery)

Heterochromia Iridis: Striking lighter-colored iris on the affected side (hypochromia) seen pathognomonically in congenital Horner syndrome or lesions acquired during infancy before ocular melanocyte pigmentation matures (sympathetic innervation is essential for normal melanocyte melanin production)

Pharmacologic Confirmation and Localization: 1) Apraclonidine 0.5% eyedrops: Reversal of anisocoria (Horner pupil dilates dramatically and ptosis lifts due to alpha-1 denervation receptor hypersensitivity, whereas normal pupil shows little/no response); 2) Cocaine 4-10% eyedrops: Confirms Horner syndrome (blocks norepinephrine reuptake; normal pupil dilates, but Horner pupil fails to dilate, worsening anisocoria); 3) Hydroxyamphetamine 1% eyedrops: Differentiates preganglionic (1st/2nd order: pupil dilates) from postganglionic (3rd order: Horner pupil fails to dilate due to degeneration of postganglionic nerve terminal stores)
radiological_manifestations: CT Angiography (CTA) or MR Angiography (MRA) of the Neck (Vascular Emergency): Critical for acute painful Horner syndrome; pathognomonically demonstrates internal carotid artery (ICA) dissection: classic 'crescent sign' (eccentric, hyperintense intramural hematoma visible on T1-weighted fat-saturated axial MRI surrounding the narrowed arterial flow void), tapered luminal narrowing ('string sign' or 'flame sign'), dissecting pseudoaneurysm, or complete vascular occlusion

High-Resolution Chest and Neck CT/MRI (Lung Apices): Critical for painless or progressive 2nd-order preganglionic Horner syndrome; pathognomonically visualizes an apical lung tumor (superior pulmonary sulcus / Pancoast tumor, typically non-small cell lung carcinoma) invading the first and second thoracic ribs, vertebral bodies, inferior trunk of the brachial plexus, and the sympathetic paravertebral chain / stellate (cervicothoracic) ganglion; or mediastinal lymphadenopathy/mass (neuroblastoma in infants)

Brain MRI with Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI): Visualizes acute lateral medullary ischemic infarction (Wallenberg syndrome) involving the descending central sympathetics in the dorsolateral medulla caused by posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or vertebral artery occlusion
Skull Base and Cavernous Sinus MRI: Identifies third-order postganglionic lesions such as cavernous sinus thrombosis, carotid-cavernous fistulas, skull base meningiomas, or petrous apex fractures
pathology_manifestations: Anatomic Pathway Disruption: 1) First-order central neuron: descends uncrossed from posterolateral hypothalamus through brainstem to the ciliospinal center of Budge-Waller in the intermediolateral cell column of C8-T2; 2) Second-order preganglionic neuron: exits C8-T2 via ventral roots, loops over the lung apex beneath the subclavian artery, and ascends the cervical sympathetic trunk to synapse in the superior cervical ganglion at C2-C3; 3) Third-order postganglionic neuron: travels in the adventitia of the internal carotid artery through the carotid canal and cavernous sinus, joining the ophthalmic division of CN V (nasociliary nerve) to reach the iris pupillodilator and Müller's tarsal muscles

Histopathology of Underlying Etiology: In apical Pancoast tumor: invasive non-small cell lung carcinoma (squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma) demonstrating malignant pleomorphic epithelial cells infiltrating perineural spaces of sympathetic nerves; in internal carotid dissection: transmural intimal tear with secondary subintimal or subadventitial dissection and intramural hematoma dissecting through the internal elastic lamina; in neuroblastoma (pediatric): small, round blue cells with fibrillary neuropil and Homer Wright pseudorosettes; in congenital Horner: stromal hypoplasia of the iris with marked depletion of stromal melanin granules
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Paramount neuro-ophthalmic syndrome featuring the pathognomonic miosis-ptosis-anhidrosis triad with reversal on apraclonidine testing, MRI carotid dissection 'crescent sign' or apical Pancoast tumor, and sympathetic denervation pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Pupillary/oculosympathetic manifestation of several diseases (dissection, Pancoast, cluster headache), not a disease.

excluded_topics.name: Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy
excluded_topics.subspecialty: Retina & Vitreous / Retinal Vascular & Metabolic Diseases
clinical_manifestations: Advanced, vision-threatening stage of diabetic eye disease occurring in both type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus, directly correlating with duration of hyperglycemia, poor glycemic control (elevated HbA1c), systemic hypertension, and diabetic nephropathy

Patients may remain asymptomatic initially despite active proliferation, or present with sudden severe visual loss, fresh dark floating cobwebs, or red haze from vitreous or preretinal hemorrhage, or slowly progressive vision distortion from tractional retinal detachment

Pathognomonic Funduscopic Hallmark: Retinal Neovascularization: delicate, frond-like, branching, abnormal new vessels breaching the internal limiting membrane: 1) Neovascularization of the Disc (NVD): new vessels on or within one disc diameter of the optic nerve head; 2) Neovascularization Elsewhere (NVE): new vessels occurring along retinal vascular arcades or elsewhere >1 disc diameter from the disc
High-Risk PDR Criteria: Defined by: 1) NVD ≥ 1/4 to 1/3 disc area; 2) Any NVD accompanied by preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage; 3) NVE ≥ 1/2 disc area accompanied by preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage

Associated Vitreoretinal Features: Preretinal (subhyaloid) hemorrhages showing distinct boat-shaped or D-shaped fluid levels; dense vitreous hemorrhage obscuring funduscopic view; progressive fibrovascular proliferation forming white, glistening fibrous sheets and bands along the posterior hyaloid face; progressive contraction of these fibrovascular bands leads to Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD: characteristically concave, immobile, tent-shaped or peaked retinal detachment that lacks retinal breaks); combined tractional-rhegmatogenous retinal detachment; rubeosis iridis (neovascularization of the iris) leading to neovascular glaucoma
radiological_manifestations: Fluorescein Angiography (FA) Pathognomonic Hallmark: Gold standard for mapping neovascularization and ischemia; demonstrates intense, early hyperfluorescence of delicate, arborizing, lace-like capillary networks (NVD and NVE) lacking tight junctions, followed by rapid, profuse, blooming late leakage of fluorescein dye that completely obscures the underlying retinal vessels; widespread peripheral and midperipheral capillary non-perfusion (ischemic capillary dropout zones); pinpoint hyperfluorescent microaneurysms; and prominent hypofluorescent blocking defects corresponding to preretinal or intraretinal hemorrhages

Spectral-Domain Optical Coherence Tomography (SD-OCT): Visualizes the vitreoretinal interface in high detail: demonstrates hyperreflective fibrovascular stalks originating from the inner retina, breaking through the internal limiting membrane (ILM), and growing along the partially detached posterior hyaloid; demonstrates anteroposterior and tangential vitreoretinal traction, tent-like tractional retinal detachment with intraretinal schisis cavities, and evaluates concurrent Diabetic Macular Edema (DME) featuring hypo-reflective intraretinal cystoid spaces in inner and outer plexiform layers, diffuse sponge-like retinal thickening, and hyperreflective intraretinal lipid foci

Optical Coherence Tomography Angiography (OCTA): Non-invasively reveals the three-dimensional arborization and origin of NVD and NVE, maps the precise extent of capillary nonperfusion in both superficial and deep capillary plexuses, and visualizes foveal avascular zone (FAZ) enlargement and capillary ring destruction

B-Scan Ocular Ultrasonography: Essential when dense vitreous hemorrhage completely blocks funduscopic view; shows low-to-medium reflective mobile echoes representing vitreous hemorrhage, and demonstrates a taut, high-amplitude, peaked, tent-like reflective membrane representing tractional retinal detachment (TRD) that remains relatively immobile on real-time kinetic testing (contrasted with the undulant, highly mobile membrane of rhegmatogenous detachment)
pathology_manifestations: Microvascular Pathophysiology: Chronic hyperglycemia triggers sorbitol accumulation (aldose reductase pathway), non-enzymatic advanced glycation end-product (AGE) formation, and protein kinase C (PKC) activation; early hallmark pathology is selective apoptosis and loss of retinal capillary pericytes ('pericyte ghosts' with a 1:1 ratio dropping to 1:10 pericyte-to-endothelial ratio) and basement membrane thickening

Ischemic Cascade and Angiogenesis: Progressive microvascular occlusion and capillary dropout cause profound retinal tissue hypoxia; hypoxia stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1a), driving massive transcriptional upregulation and intraocular secretion of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF-A) and angiopoietin-2

Histopathology of Neovascularization: Fragile endothelial cell cords breach the internal limiting membrane (ILM) and proliferate into the potential space between the ILM and the posterior vitreous cortex; neovascular fronds lack mature pericytes and tight junctional complexes (yielding high permeability); transdifferentiation of surrounding hyalocytes and glial cells into alpha-smooth muscle actin-positive myofibroblasts generates contractile fibrovascular scaffolds that exert mechanical traction on the neurosensory retina
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Archetypal metabolic-vascular ocular disease displaying pathognomonic retinal neovascular fronds (NVD/NVE) with profuse FA leakage, SD-OCT fibrovascular traction/DME, and pericyte loss/VEGF-driven angiogenesis pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Retinal manifestation of diabetes mellitus. Diabetes was excluded as a general non-visual topic; its single fundus complication should not re-enter as its own topic.

excluded_topics.name: Freiberg Infraction
clinical_manifestations: Localized pain, exquisite point tenderness, and firm dorsal soft-tissue tumefaction directly over the second metatarsal head (in 80% of cases; less commonly the third metatarsal head in 15%, rarely fourth)
Palpable, hard, bony enlargement and thickening of the affected metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint on circumferential palpation
Weight-bearing antalgic gait: Patient ambulates with a characteristic 'heel-walking' or lateral foot-border loading pattern to avoid forefoot push-off (avoidance of forefoot loading)
Exacerbation by footwear: Pain intensely aggravated by barefoot walking on hard surfaces or wearing narrow, elevated high-heeled footwear that forces excessive hyperextension across the MTP joints
Range of motion restriction: Painful, guarded limitation of passive MTP joint motion, particularly restricted dorsiflexion, with palpable intra-articular crepitus in advanced stages

Demographic predisposition: Marked predilection for adolescent and young adult females (female-to-male ratio of 4:1 to 5:1, typically presenting between ages 11 and 18 during the pubertal growth spurt)
radiological_manifestations: Weight-Bearing Anteroposterior (AP), Lateral, and Oblique Foot Radiographs - Smillie Classification (Five Sequential Stages): Stage I: Faint, subtle radiolucent fracture fissure through the subchondral bone of the dorsal epiphysis of the metatarsal head; Stage II: Central articular depression and flattening of the dorsal aspect of the metatarsal head with apparent widening of the MTP joint space; Stage III: Further central osteochondral depression with absorption of subchondral bone and formation of prominent medial and lateral articular bony projections ('peaking' or 'ears'); Stage IV: Complete structural collapse of the metatarsal head with separation of a loose, detached central osteochondral fragment into the joint space; Stage V: Advanced degenerative post-infraction osteoarthritis characterized by profound joint space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, flattening, and pronounced cortical thickening/hypertrophy of the metatarsal shaft

Forefoot MRI: Highly sensitive for early pre-radiographic infarction (Stage I): Low signal intensity on T1-weighted images and high signal intensity on T2/STIR images localized to the subchondral bone marrow of the metatarsal head; precisely outlines articular cartilage integrity, presence of detached loose bodies, and degree of subchondral collapse
pathology_manifestations: Vascular and Biomechanical Etiopathogenesis: Repetitive shear and compressive microtrauma combined with focal microvascular compromise; the second metatarsal is anatomically the longest and most rigid ray (mortised securely into the cuneiforms), absorbing the highest ground reaction forces during the terminal push-off phase of the gait cycle

Histopathology of the Epiphysis: Avascular osteonecrosis of the subchondral cancellous bone marked by empty osteocyte lacunae and necrotic medullary fatty marrow; multiple microfractures occurring along the subchondral bony plate followed by fracture non-union and dorsal articular surface depression; formation of fibrocartilaginous metaplasia, unorganized vascular granulation tissue, and osteoclastic resorption along the perimeter, leading to detachment of a free intra-articular osteochondral fragment
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Cardinal adolescent osteochondrosis of the second metatarsal head presenting with dorsal forefoot pain, palpable head enlargement, and an antalgic heel-loading gait, staged radiographically by Smillie criteria from dorsal flattening to joint collapse.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Osteochondrosis seen on foot radiographs, without a disease-specific photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Neuropathic Arthropathy (Charcot Joint)
clinical_manifestations: Profound, massive, warm, erythematous, edematous swelling of the foot or ankle that is remarkably painless or mild relative to the destructive severity
Collapse of the tarsometatarsal architecture producing a convex plantar midfoot deformity ('rocker-bottom foot')
Audible and palpable bone-grinding crepitus upon weight-bearing
Chronic non-healing plantar neuropathic ulcerations over displaced bony prominences
Absence of protective sensory perception (monofilament testing)
radiological_manifestations: Plain Radiographs of Foot/Ankle: The classic '6 Ds' of neuropathic joint destruction: Distension (joint effusion), Disorganization (loss of normal alignment), Dislocation, Debris (abundant intra-articular bony fragments), Destruction (subchondral bone resorption), and Density (dense reactive sclerosis); severe tarsometatarsal (Lisfranc) collapse

MRI of Foot: Disruption of capsuloligamentous structures, widespread bone marrow edema, periarticular fluid collections; differentiation from osteomyelitis (absence of sinus tracts tracking to marrow)
pathology_manifestations: Joint resection histology: Extensive intra-articular fragmentation of articular cartilage and subchondral bone, embedding of tiny bone shards into hyperplastic synovial lining ('detritus'), dense subchondral sclerosis, and marked lack of acute suppurative inflammation
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Unmistakable bedside 'rocker-bottom foot' and gross structural collapse paired with the textbook '6 Ds' of devastating radiographic bone fragmentation and dislocation on plain film.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Neuroarthropathy is a manifestation of neuropathy (often diabetes or syphilis), not a primary disease.

excluded_topics.name: Osgood-Schlatter Disease
synonyms: traction apophysitis of the tibial tuberosity
clinical_manifestations: Prominent, visible, and palpable tender bony enlargement and swelling directly over the tibial tuberosity in an active, rapidly growing adolescent (typical age: boys 12-15 years, girls 10-13 years; frequently bilateral in 20-30% of patients)
Exquisite focal point tenderness elicited by direct palpation of the secondary ossification center of the tibial tuberosity and distal patellar tendon attachment

Pain provocation tests: Sharp anterior knee pain reproduced by resisted active knee extension from a flexed position, or during passive extreme knee flexion (stretching the quadriceps extensor mechanism)

Activity-related exacerbation: Severe pain triggered by high-impact quadriceps-loading activities (jumping, sprinting, kicking, stair climbing, squatting, or kneeling directly on hard surfaces; highly prevalent in basketball, soccer, volleyball, and gymnastics athletes)

Musculoskeletal exam findings: Prominent tightness and inflexibility of the quadriceps and hamstring muscle groups; overlying skin warmth and soft-tissue tumefaction without true intra-articular joint effusion
radiological_manifestations: Lateral Knee Radiograph: Pathognomonic fragmentation and irregular ossification of the secondary ossification center (apophysis) of the tibial tuberosity; prominent soft-tissue swelling overlying the tibial tubercle with effacement and loss of the sharp radiolucent triangular contour of the infrapatellar (Hoffa's) fat pad; separation, elevation, or anterior displacement of cortical osseous fragments/ossicles from the underlying tibial metaphysis; formation of mature, separate heterotopic ossicles within the substance of the distal patellar tendon

High-Resolution Knee Ultrasound: Thickening, hypoechogenicity, and loss of normal fibrillar architecture of the distal patellar tendon insertion; deep infrapatellar bursitis (distended bursa with anechoic/hypoechoic fluid adjacent to the tubercle); Power Doppler demonstrates marked hypervascularity and neovascularization at the bone-tendon junction; direct acoustic visualization of cartilaginous avulsion clefts and mobile apophyseal bony fragments

Knee MRI (indicated for atypical or recalcitrant cases): Extensive bone marrow edema (hypointense on T1, hyperintense on T2/STIR) within the tibial tuberosity and adjacent anterior proximal tibial metaphysis; high-signal inflammatory edema within the distal patellar tendon, Hoffa fat pad, and deep infrapatellar bursa
pathology_manifestations: Traction Micro-Avulsion Apophysitis: Repetitive, concentrated mechanical tensile traction exerted by the quadriceps extensor mechanism via the patellar tendon onto the biomechanically vulnerable, partially ossified secondary growth center (apophysis) of the tibial tuberosity during rapid skeletal growth spurts

Histopathology of Resected Tubercle/Ossicle: Microfractures through the cartilaginous and fibrocartilaginous zone of the apophysis with patchy areas of ischemic cartilage necrosis; robust reparative response featuring hypercellular fibrovascular granulation tissue, reactive chondrogenesis, and immature woven bone formation

Non-Union and Ossicle Formation: Chronic non-union of the avulsed fragment leading to endochondral ossification within the tendon, producing a detached, permanent accessory bony ossicle that can cause persistent kneeling pain into adulthood
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Cardinal pediatric traction apophysitis causing a tender, visible tibial tubercle enlargement in athletic adolescents, diagnosed radiologically by apophyseal fragmentation and patellar tendon thickening, and caused by micro-avulsion injuries at the chondro-osseous junction.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Traction apophysitis. Swelling and a fragmented tubercle are a finding, not a disease gallery.

excluded_topics.name: Asbestosis and Asbestos-Related Pleural Disease
clinical_manifestations: Prominent digital clubbing in advanced stages
Bibasilar end-inspiratory crackles
Cyanosis and signs of cor pulmonale (elevated JVP, peripheral edema)
