radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography / CT: Bilateral, well-circumscribed, multi-focal pleural plaques along the posterolateral mid-chest wall and dome of the diaphragm; pathognomonic dense calcification of diaphragmatic plaques ('holly leaf' pattern)

Chest HRCT: Subpleural linear bands ('dot and line' pattern), parenchymal bands radiating to the pleura ('crow's feet'), basilar subpleural reticulation and honeycombing mimicking UIP, diffuse pleural thickening
pathology_manifestations: Lung biopsy / Bronchoalveolar lavage: Asbestos bodies (golden-brown, beaded, dumbbell-shaped ferruginous bodies formed by asbestos fibers coated with iron-protein complexes, highlighted by Prussian blue iron stain); interstitial fibrosis surrounding respiratory bronchioles
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Features digital clubbing and cyanosis alongside the pathognomonic 'holly-leaf' calcified diaphragmatic pleural plaques and subpleural curvilinear lines on chest CT.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Occupational imaging/pleural-plaque diagnosis without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Bronchopulmonary Sequestration
clinical_manifestations: Recurrent, localized, treatment-refractory lower-lobe bacterial pneumonia (fever, purulent sputum, productive cough) classically restricted to the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe (65%) or right lower lobe

Episodic hemoptysis ranging from recurrent blood-streaked sputum to life-threatening massive pulmonary hemorrhage due to high systemic-pressure arterial perfusion supplying fragile parenchymal capillary beds
Continuous vascular murmur or systolic bruit occasionally audible on chest auscultation over the lower posterior hemithorax / paravertebral region, accentuating during inspiration
Neonatal respiratory distress, tachypnea, grunting, and central cyanosis in neonates presenting with large extralobar sequestrations or high-output arteriovenous shunts
Digital clubbing, asthenic habitus, and failure to thrive in undiagnosed children or young adults with chronic, suppurative intralobar sequestration
radiological_manifestations: Chest CT Angiography (CTA - Gold Standard): Conclusively demonstrates an anomalous, aberrant systemic arterial feeding vessel arising directly from the descending thoracic aorta (80%), upper abdominal aorta (15%), or celiac/subclavian arteries, entering a non-functioning, non-aerated lung mass; delineates venous drainage into pulmonary veins (95% of intralobar sequestrations) or into systemic veins such as the azygos, hemiazygos, or inferior vena cava (extralobar sequestrations)

Chest HRCT: Well-circumscribed, solid, or multicystic mass in the posterior basal segment of the lower lobe; cystic lesions often demonstrate variable air-fluid levels (indicating secondary fistulous communication with the bronchial tree via infection), surrounded by hyperlucent emphysematous lung parenchyma due to collateral air drift

Chest Radiography (CXR): Triangular, oval, or round well-defined retrocardiac opacity in the medial or posterior aspect of the left lower lung base (less commonly right base), occasionally simulating a congenital diaphragmatic hernia, lung abscess, or hydropneumothorax

Fetal / Neonatal Thoracic Ultrasound with Color Doppler: Hyperechoic, solid triangular intrathoracic mass in the lower chest with clear color Doppler visualization of systemic arterial flow directly from the descending aorta
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology (Intralobar vs. Extralobar): Intralobar sequestration (75%) shares the visceral pleural investment of the surrounding normal lung; Extralobar sequestration (25%) is completely invested in its own separate, distinct visceral pleural envelope, frequently located between the lower lobe and diaphragm or subdiaphragmatically

Histopathology: Disorganized, non-aerated embryonic or dysplastic pulmonary parenchyma with variable cystic dilation of bronchioles and bronchi lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar or cuboidal epithelium; prominent chronic interstitial inflammation, fibrosis, alveolar accumulation of foamy lipid-laden macrophages (endogenous lipoid pneumonia), and complete absence of normal communication with the native bronchial tree

Vascular Histology: Aberrant feeding vessel exhibits characteristic thick, muscularized elastic systemic arterial wall structure prone to atherosclerosis, aneurysm formation, or thrombosis under persistent high systemic arterial pressures
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Classic congenital thoracic malformation defined by the pathognomonic CTA demonstration of an aberrant systemic arterial feeder arising directly from the descending aorta supplying a non-communicating lower-lobe mass, correlating with recurrent localized hemoptysis, murmurs, and dysplastic sequestered histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: CT/angiographic congenital lesion without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Congenital Lobar Emphysema
clinical_manifestations: Acute or subacute respiratory distress in early infancy (over 80% presenting before 6 months of age, with 50% symptomatic within the first days of life): marked tachypnea, grunting, intercostal and subcostal retractions, and nasal flaring
Feeding intolerance: cyanosis, choking, and severe paroxysmal coughing triggered by nursing or bottle feeding due to gastroesophageal and tracheobronchial compression
Strikingly asymmetric physical exam findings: Visible bulging, asymmetrical prominence, and hyperexpansion of the affected hemithorax with widened intercostal spaces

Chest Percussion and Auscultation: Markedly hyperresonant or tympanitic percussion note with profoundly diminished or completely absent vesicular breath sounds over the overexpanded lobe; contralateral tracheal tug and displaced cardiac apical impulse

Life-threatening acute respiratory failure: Severe respiratory acidosis and hemodynamic compromise developing from high intrathoracic pressure impairing systemic venous return (cardiac tamponade physiology)
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography (Diagnostic Hallmark): Massive, hyperlucent, hyperinflated single lobe with attenuated, stretched, and widely spaced bronchovascular markings; striking herniation of the overinflated lobe across the anterior superior mediastinum into the opposite hemithorax ('anterior mediastinal herniation sign')

Contralateral Mediastinal Shift: Marked displacement of the heart and mediastinal structures away from the affected side, with severe compressive atelectasis and collapse of the adjacent ipsilateral lobes (e.g., lower lobe) and the contralateral lung; ipsilateral hemidiaphragmatic depression and flattening
Anatomic Lobar Distribution: Left upper lobe is most commonly affected (40–50%), followed by right middle lobe (30–35%), and right upper lobe (20%); lower lobes are extremely rarely involved (<2%)

Chest CT (High-Resolution): Confirms marked hyperinflation of the affected lobe without parenchymal destruction; demonstrates the stretched, sparse pulmonary vessels and allows precise evaluation of tracheobronchial branching and extrinsic vascular compression (e.g., aberrant left pulmonary artery, pulmonary sling, or large patent ductus arteriosus)

Early Neonatal Radiographic Evolution: During the first 24–48 hours of life, the affected lobe may initially appear opacified or hazy due to delayed clearance of fetal lung liquid trapped by the bronchial obstruction ('opaque lobar emphysema'), which progressively clears to reveal classic hyperlucency
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Non-Destructive Alveolar Overinflation): Striking, uniform overdistension and marked enlargement of alveoli (often 3 to 10 times normal alveolar diameter) with intact, stretched alveolar walls; critically lacks the alveolar wall destruction, necrosis, and fibrosis seen in true adult destructive emphysema ('alveolar overinflation' rather than true emphysema)

Bronchial Cartilage Pathology: Intrinsic developmental bronchial cartilage defect in 50% of cases, consisting of localized bronchomalacia, hypoplasia, fragmentation, or complete absence of bronchial cartilage rings in the lobar or segmental bronchus; allows dynamic airway collapse during expiration (ball-valve mechanism) leading to progressive air trapping
Extrinsic Vascular Compression: In 10–15% of cases, an anomalous systemic or pulmonary vessel compresses the bronchus externally
Polyalveolar Lobe: In a subset of patients, the number of alveoli per acinus is markedly increased (polyalveolar lobe, >5 times normal alveolar count) despite normal architecture
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Premier pediatric thoracic emergency showing neonatal asymmetric chest bulging, tympany, and cyanosis, diagnosed by classic massive single-lobe hyperinflation with anterior mediastinal herniation on CXR/CT and bronchial cartilage dysplasia on pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Neonatal radiographic diagnosis without a disease-specific photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Congenital Pulmonary Airway Malformation
synonyms: congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung
clinical_manifestations: Acute neonatal respiratory distress: progressive tachypnea (respiratory rate >60 breaths/min), expiratory grunting, deep sternal and subcostal retractions, and nasal flaring developing within minutes to hours after birth
Central cyanosis of the lips, tongue, and nailbeds refractory to supplemental oxygen, reflecting severe ventilation-perfusion mismatch and ipsilateral/contralateral pulmonary hypoplasia
Asymmetric thoracic cage expansion with visible bulging and hyperexpansion of the affected hemithorax, accompanied by contralateral displacement of the apical cardiac impulse

Auscultation: Unilaterally absent or markedly decreased vesicular breath sounds over the affected hemithorax, with hyperresonance (in cystic types) or dullness (in solid/microcystic types) on percussion

In utero / peripartum non-immune hydrops fetalis: generalized anasarca, scalp edema, pleural effusion, and ascites due to inferior vena cava and cardiac compression from a massive intrathoracic mass (high CPAM volume ratio >1.6)
Recurrent intractable pneumonia, lung abscess, or episodic wheezing and hemoptysis in late-presenting older children and adults
radiological_manifestations: Chest HRCT / Contrast CT (Diagnostic Reference Standard): Detailed architectural characterization according to the Stocker classification: Type 1 (50-60%: single or multiple dominant large thin-walled cysts 2–10 cm in diameter with occasional air-fluid levels); Type 2 (15-20%: multiple uniform smaller cysts 0.5–2 cm mimicking bronchiectasis, frequently associated with other congenital anomalies); Type 3 (10%: bulky, solid-appearing, microcystic lesions <0.5 cm producing massive mediastinal shift and parenchymal compression); Type 4 (large peripheral, thin-walled cysts >10 cm difficult to distinguish from pleuropulmonary blastoma)

Chest Radiography: Multilocular cystic intrathoracic mass containing air- and fluid-filled cavities, causing pronounced contralateral mediastinal and cardiac shift, depression and flattening of the ipsilateral hemidiaphragm, and compressive atelectasis of the adjacent normal lung lobes

Prenatal Ultrasound / Fetal MRI: Echogenic or multiseptated cystic thoracic mass; enables calculation of the CPAM Volume Ratio (CVR = [length × width × height × 0.52] / head circumference), where CVR >1.6 reliably predicts increased risk of hydrops fetalis requiring in utero intervention
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Stocker Classification): Characterized by an adenomatoid proliferation of terminal respiratory bronchiole-like structures with an absence of normal alveolar development; cystic structures lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar (Type 1), simple cuboidal (Type 2), or non-ciliated cuboidal epithelium (Type 3)

Characteristic mucigenic cells: Type 1 cysts frequently feature clusters of mucin-producing columnar cells (mucous metaplasia) that stain intensely positive with Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) and Alcian blue

Stromal alterations: Cyst walls are composed of fibromuscular stroma containing abundant elastic fibers, but characteristically lack bronchial cartilage plates (excluding true bronchogenic cysts) and demonstrate no peribronchial mucous glands; absence of primitive blastemal mesenchymal spindle cells (differentiating from pleuropulmonary blastoma [PPB], DICER1-negative)
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic congenital bronchopulmonary dysplastic disorder presenting with neonatal respiratory distress, cyanosis, and hemithorax bulging, validated by pathognomonic multilocular cystic lesions with contralateral mediastinal shift on HRCT/CXR and adenomatoid bronchiolar histology lacking cartilage.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Prenatal/CT cystic lung lesion without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Mounier-Kuhn Syndrome (Tracheobronchomegaly)
clinical_manifestations: Distinctive loud, deep, booming, harsh 'barking' or 'seal-like' chronic cough caused by turbulent airflow within the massively dilated central airways
Expectoration of copious amounts of purulent, foul-smelling sputum with recurrent episodes of lower respiratory tract infections and pneumonia
Visible severe inspiratory intercostal, suprasternal, and substernal retractions, accompanied by loud low-pitched tracheal breath sounds heard even without a stethoscope
Severe digital clubbing and central cyanosis in advanced disease with chronic secondary bronchiectasis

Direct bronchoscopic visual inspection (pathognomonic visual findings): massive, cavernous enlargement of the trachea and mainstem bronchi, broad intercartilaginous mucosal herniations forming multiple tracheal diverticula, and dramatic expiratory dynamic airway collapse (>70–100%) as the posterior membrane herniates forward into the lumen
radiological_manifestations: Chest HRCT (Diagnostic Gold Standard): Marked, pathological dilation of the trachea and main bronchi exceeding standard diagnostic cutoffs: transverse tracheal diameter >25 mm (females) or >30 mm (males); sagittal tracheal diameter >27 mm (females) or >32 mm (males); right mainstem bronchus >19.8 mm (females) or >24 mm (males); left mainstem bronchus >17.4 mm (females) or >23 mm (males); characteristic scalloped, undulating tracheal contour with broad outpouchings (diverticulosis) protruding between cartilaginous rings; lower-lobe cylindrical, varicose, and cystic bronchiectasis

Dynamic Paired Inspiratory-Expiratory CT: Striking dynamic tracheobronchomalacia demonstrating >50–80% collapse of tracheal and bronchial luminal cross-sectional area during forced expiration or coughing
Chest Radiography: Readily visible enlargement of the tracheal air column extending from the subglottic region to the carina, with widening of the subcarinal angle
pathology_manifestations: Tracheal and bronchial wall histology (Autopsy / surgical specimens): Marked congenital or acquired atrophy, fragmentation, or complete absence of the longitudinal elastic fibers and smooth muscle layers (muscularis mucosae) within the tracheobronchial wall; thinning, attenuation, and outward displacement of the cartilaginous rings, permitting mucosal herniation between the rings; chronic mononuclear inflammatory infiltrates with secondary squamous metaplasia and goblet cell hyperplasia of the airway epithelium
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Rare airway condition featuring a booming 'barking' cough and dynamic bronchoscopic airway collapse, paired with pathognomonic massive tracheobronchial dilatation and intercartilaginous diverticula on chest HRCT.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Airway-caliber imaging diagnosis without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Pancoast Tumor (Superior Pulmonary Sulcus Tumor)
clinical_manifestations: Pathognomonic Pancoast-Tobias triad: (1) severe, unrelenting shoulder and medial scapular pain, (2) radicular arm pain with hand weakness/atrophy along the C8-T1 nerve root distribution, and (3) ipsilateral Horner's syndrome

Classic Horner's Syndrome (Physical Signs): Unilateral ptosis (drooping eyelid due to denervation of Müller's muscle), miosis (constricted pupil from loss of pupillary dilator tone), facial anhidrosis (absence of sweating over the ipsilateral hemiface and neck), and apparent enophthalmos caused by tumor invasion of the paravertebral sympathetic chain and stellate (inferior cervical) ganglion

Lower Brachial Plexopathy: Severe burning and radiating pain along the medial arm, forearm, fourth and fifth digits (ulnar distribution); marked muscle wasting and atrophy of the intrinsic hand muscles (thenar/hypothenar eminences, interossei) leading to claw-hand deformity and loss of grip strength

Thoracic Outlet and Vascular Compression: Asymmetric unilateral upper-extremity edema, cyanosis, and dilated superficial collateral veins over the shoulder and chest wall from subclavian vein compression; reduced or absent radial pulse from subclavian artery compression
Supraclavicular lymphadenopathy: Firm, fixed, non-tender palpable mass in the supraclavicular fossa on bedside examination
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography (CXR): Asymmetrical apical pleural thickening, apical cap opacity (>5 mm), or soft-tissue mass in the extreme apex of the lung; focal destruction or osteolytic erosion of the posterior aspect of the 1st, 2nd, or 3rd ribs and adjacent transverse processes (often overlooked on early chest films as subtle apical scarring)

Contrast-Enhanced Chest CT: Delineates an invasive, irregular apical soft-tissue mass occupying the thoracic inlet; demonstrates cortical destruction of the superior rib cage, invasion into adjacent vertebral bodies, and compression of subclavian and brachiocephalic vessels

Magnetic Resonance Imaging (Thoracic Inlet MRI - Gold Standard for Staging): Superior soft-tissue resolution specifically demonstrates tumor infiltration into the C8, T1, and T2 nerve roots and lower trunk of the brachial plexus; delineates invasion of the stellate ganglion, vertebral artery, subclavian artery and vein, and epidural extension into the neural foramina and spinal canal
18F-FDG PET/CT: Intense hypermetabolic uptake in the apical mass and evaluates mediastinal lymph node staging and distant metastases (bone, brain, adrenal)
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Tumor Subtypes): Predominantly non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) originating from the peripheral apical lung parenchyma: Squamous cell carcinoma (45–50%) and Adenocarcinoma (35–40%); Large cell carcinoma (10%); Small cell lung cancer is distinctly rare (<3–5%)

Microscopic Features: Infiltrative nests and sheets of malignant epithelial cells demonstrating prominent cytologic atypia, hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei, and brisk mitotic activity; squamous cell carcinomas feature diagnostic intracellular keratinization, intercellular bridges, and keratin pearls; adenocarcinomas display glandular formation and intracytoplasmic mucin

Invasion Characteristics: Direct, aggressive perineural invasion infiltrating surrounding nerve sheaths (brachial plexus trunk, sympathetic trunk), with destructive infiltration into periosteum, cortical bone, skeletal muscle fibers, and regional neurovascular bundles

Immunohistochemistry: TTF-1 and Napsin A positive in adenocarcinoma; p40 and CK5/6 strongly positive in squamous cell carcinoma; EGFR, ALK, ROS1, and PD-L1 testing guides targeted oncologic management
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Exemplary apical thoracic neoplasm defined by the textbook bedside Pancoast-Tobias syndrome (Horner's syndrome, intrinsic hand muscle atrophy, C8-T1 radiculopathy) corroborated by apical mass with rib osteolysis on CXR/CT and brachial plexus invasion on MRI.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Regional manifestation of apical lung cancer (Horner syndrome, hand wasting), not a separate disease.

excluded_topics.name: Scimitar Syndrome (Congenital Pulmonary Venolobar Syndrome)
synonyms: partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection (PAPVC) with hypoplastic lung
clinical_manifestations: Asymmetrical Thoracic Examination: Hypoplasia of the right hemithorax with noticeable flattening, decreased thoracic circumference, and reduced chest wall expansion on the right side

Dextroposition of the Heart: Apical cardiac impulse shifted rightward toward the sternal border or right fifth intercostal space (cardiac shift secondary to right lung hypoplasia, without true situs inversus)

Cardiac Murmurs: Systolic ejection murmur audible at the left upper sternal border with wide, fixed splitting of the second heart sound (S2), reflecting right ventricular volume overload from a left-to-right shunt (associated ostium secundum atrial septal defect [ASD] present in 70%)
Vascular Bruit: Soft continuous vascular bruit occasionally audible over the right lower posterior chest wall or infrascapular area, corresponding to systemic arterial collateral flow

Clinical Presentation Forms: Infantile Form: Severe heart failure, tachypnea, failure to thrive, and severe pulmonary hypertension presenting in the first months of life; Adult/Childhood Form: Recurrent right lower-lobe pneumonia, exertional dyspnea, fatigue, or asymptomatic incidental diagnosis
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography (The Pathognomonic 'Scimitar Sign'): A prominent, vertically oriented, curvilinear anomalous pulmonary vein descending parallel to the right cardiac border toward the cardiophrenic angle to drain into the inferior vena cava, bearing an uncanny resemblance to the curved blade of an Ottoman Turkish sword (scimitar); hypoplastic right hemithorax with elevation of the right hemidiaphragm and rightward shift of the heart and mediastinum

Multidetector CT Angiography (CTA - Gold Standard): Flawlessly tracks the course of the anomalous scimitar vein from the right pulmonary parenchyma as it courses caudally through the diaphragm to empty into the suprahepatic inferior vena cava (IVC), cavoatrial junction, or right atrium; accurately identifies systemic arterial collaterals arising from the subdiaphragmatic abdominal aorta supplying the right lower lobe

Vascular Hypoplasia on CTA: Demonstrates hypoplasia or complete atresia of the right pulmonary artery with diminished right-sided pulmonary vascular markings and compensatory hypertrophy of the left pulmonary artery

Associated Lung Anomalies: Delineates right lung hypoplasia, bronchial segmentation anomalies (moniliform bronchus, bronchial isomerism), horseshoe lung (fusion of posterior basal segments across the midline), and secondary bronchiectasis

Cardiac MRI: Accurately calculates the systemic-to-pulmonary shunt fraction (Qp:Qs ratio), delineates anomalous venous anatomy, and evaluates right ventricular dilation and ejection fraction without ionizing radiation
pathology_manifestations: Gross Pathology: Hypogenetic right lung: markedly reduced weight and volume, frequently consisting of only two lobes (mirroring a normal left lung) or possessing a single dysmorphic lobe; absent or incomplete interlobar fissures; prominent anomalous venous trunk descending through the inferior pulmonary ligament

Vascular Histology: The anomalous scimitar vein exhibits thick fibromuscular walls with medial hypertrophy; systemic arterial feeders from the aorta demonstrate robust elastic systemic arterial architecture with intimal thickening and medial muscular hyperplasia, subjected to systemic arterial pressure

Pulmonary Parenchyma: Reduced number of bronchopulmonary segments and simplified alveolar architecture with deficient acinar branching; medial hypertrophy and muscularization of pulmonary arterioles in cases with severe precapillary and postcapillary pulmonary hypertension
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Prototypic congenital venolobar anomaly featuring right-sided chest hypoplasia, dextroposition, and left-to-right shunt murmur, hallmarked by the iconic 'scimitar sign' anomalous vein on CXR/CTA and pulmonary hypoplasia on gross pathology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Chest-radiograph vascular anomaly without a photographic phenotype.

excluded_topics.name: Silicosis and Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis
clinical_manifestations: Progressive exertional dyspnea, barrel chest, and marked cachexia
Central cyanosis, tachypnea, and prominent digital clubbing (in accelerated silicosis)
Melanoptysis (expectoration of black inky sputum in coal workers' progressive massive fibrosis)
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography / CT: Multiple well-defined centrilobular and subpleural micronodules (2-5 mm) with marked upper- and posterior-zone predominance; coalescence into large bilateral conglomerate masses (Progressive Massive Fibrosis [PMF]) with compensatory emphysema
Mediastinal / Hilar CT: 'Eggshell calcification' (thin, rim-like peripheral shell calcification around enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes, pathognomonic for silicosis)
pathology_manifestations: Lung histology: Classic silicotic nodules featuring a central concentric, whorled zone of hyalinized, dense, acellular collagen surrounded by a cellular peripheral mantle of macrophages and lymphocytes; birefringent silica crystals visible under polarized light
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Shows severe clinical respiratory cachexia and melanoptysis paired with the pathognomonic 'eggshell calcification' of hilar lymph nodes and progressive massive fibrosis on chest CT.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Occupational radiographic diagnosis (nodules, eggshell nodes) without a clinical photograph.

excluded_topics.name: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome
clinical_manifestations: Pemberton's sign (pathognomonic bedside maneuver): dramatic facial plethora, flushing, cyanosis, and severe jugular venous distention precipitated within 60 seconds of bilateral arm elevation above the head until touching the ears
Profound, brawny, non-pitting edema of the face, neck, bilateral upper extremities, and periorbital tissues ('collar of Stokes')
Marked superficial venous engorgement: prominent, tortuous, serpentine collateral venous network ('caput medusae' of the anterior chest wall and shoulder girdles) with downward venous blood flow
Conjunctival suffusion, chemosis, proptosis, and glossal swelling causing hoarseness and stridor
Cerebral venous congestion symptoms: headache, dizziness, visual blurring, stupor, and syncope exacerbated by bending forward or lying supine
radiological_manifestations: Contrast-Enhanced Chest CT (Imaging Gold Standard): Direct visualization of severe luminal stenosis, complete extrinsic compression, or intraluminal filling defect (thrombus) within the superior vena cava; dramatic enhancement of extensive collateral venous pathways, including the azygos-hemiazygos system, internal mammary (internal thoracic) veins, lateral thoracic veins, vertebral venous plexus, and subcutaneous anterior chest wall collaterals; pathognomonic CT 'hot spot' sign (intense focal enhancement in the quadrate lobe / Segment IV of the liver resulting from systemic-to-portal venous shunting via the recanalized vein of Sappey or internal mammary-phrenic collaterals); identification of the causative mass (e.g., right upper lobe lung carcinoma, bulky prevascular mediastinal lymphoma, substernal goiter, or fibrosing mediastinitis)
Chest Radiography: Widening of the superior mediastinum (>8 cm), right paratracheal fullness, pleural effusion (predominantly right-sided), and right upper lobe pulmonary consolidation or mass
Superior Vena Cavography (Catheter Angiography): Real-time fluoroscopic depiction of the obstruction site, pressure gradient measurement, and direct roadmap for endovascular stenting
pathology_manifestations: Core needle / mediastinal / bronchoscopic biopsy of causative lesion: Most frequently small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC) showing sheets of small, round-to-oval cells with scant cytoplasm, finely granular 'salt-and-pepper' chromatin, nuclear molding, high mitotic rate, and Azzopardi effect (DNA incrustation in vessel walls), positive for CD56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin; non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC) showing squamous cell nests or glandular architecture; or fibrosing mediastinitis featuring dense, hypocellular, hyalinized collagenous bundles obliterating vascular structures with chronic granulomatous or lymphocytic infiltration
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Vivid thoracic vascular emergency presenting with iconic bedside signs (Pemberton sign, 'collar of Stokes' edema, and anterior chest wall venous collaterals) coupled with diagnostic contrast CT demonstrating SVC occlusion, collateral opacification, and hepatic hot spot sign.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Obstructive manifestation of thoracic malignancy or thrombosis.

excluded_topics.name: Swyer-James-MacLeod Syndrome
clinical_manifestations: Strikingly asymmetric respiratory examination: markedly reduced or absent vesicular breath sounds over the affected hemithorax compared to the normal contralateral lung, with hyperresonance to percussion
Chronic productive cough with purulent sputum, recurrent unilateral lower respiratory tract infections, and low-grade hemoptysis in patients with secondary bronchiectasis

Exertional dyspnea and reduced exercise tolerance out of proportion to clinical wheezing, often with a documented history of severe necrotizing childhood bronchiolitis or pneumonia (adenovirus types 3, 7, 21; measles; or Mycoplasma pneumoniae)
Digital clubbing (Hippocratic fingers) present in patients with extensive chronic cystic or varicose bronchiectasis
Asymmetric chest wall excursion on deep inspiration, with lag or decreased mobility of the affected hemithorax
radiological_manifestations: Chest Radiography (CXR): Classic pathognomonic triad: (1) Unilateral hyperlucent lung or lobe, (2) normal or noticeably decreased volume of the affected lung (differentiating it from congenital lobar emphysema or foreign body obstruction, where the lung is hyperinflated), and (3) marked reduction in size and arborization of the ipsilateral pulmonary hilar and peripheral vascular markings ('pruned tree' appearance)

Chest HRCT (Inspiratory vs. Expiratory Imaging - Gold Standard): Inspiratory scans reveal unilateral lung/lobar hyperlucency with attenuated, diminutive pulmonary vessels; End-expiratory scans demonstrate severe, striking geographic air-trapping where the affected lung fails to deflate and remains lucent, causing shift of the mediastinum toward the unaffected normal lung during expiration

CT Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA): Marked hypoplasia and decreased caliber of the ipsilateral pulmonary artery and its branches with severely attenuated peripheral vascularity (hypoperfusion reflexly induced by chronic alveolar hypoxia and capillary bed obliteration)
Associated Airway Findings: Coexisting cylindrical, varicose, or saccular bronchiectasis with bronchial wall thickening, mucus impaction, and mosaic attenuation

Radionuclide Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) Scintigraphy: Matched, severe unilateral defect with absent or markedly delayed xenon-133 ventilation and severely diminished or absent technetium-99m macroaggregated albumin (99mTc-MAA) perfusion in the hyperlucent lung
pathology_manifestations: Histopathology (Constrictive / Obliterative Bronchiolitis): Severe, concentric submucosal fibrosis and cicatricial scarring leading to partial or total luminal obliteration of membranous and respiratory bronchioles (<1 mm diameter); characteristic peribronchiolar chronic lymphocytic inflammation

Alveolar Architecture: Alveoli are grossly intact, overinflated, and simplified, but show NO destructive proteolytic destruction of alveolar septa (confirming non-destructive panacinar hyperinflation, unlike tobacco-induced emphysema)

Vascular Pathology: Marked secondary hypoplasia and muscular medial atrophy of pulmonary arterial branches, with fibroelastosis of pulmonary arterioles secondary to chronic disuse and reduced blood flow
excluded_topics.inclusion_rationale: Definitive post-infectious pediatric/adult entity hallmarked by unilateral hyperlucent small lung with expiratory air-trapping and hypoplastic pulmonary artery on HRCT/CTPA, matching asymmetric breath sounds and bronchiolitis obliterans histology.
excluded_topics.audit_reason: Unilateral hyperlucent-lung radiographic diagnosis.
